Mr. Labouchere is endeavouring to obtain for Mrs. Grimwood some official recognition of the valuable services pluckily rendered by her during the Manipur occurrences. He has been iiwommuni- cation with the Indian Office on the sultbct.

Peebles' is backing up Paisley in its protest against the -establishment.of diplomatic relations with the Vatican. On Monday a petition from Peebles praying that such intentions laight be fore- gone waspresented end ordered to lie on the table.

Time has not yet !permitted the receipt of letters from Lord Rancidlt3h Churchill. A. private com- munication has beeu received by telegraph by a member elf his family announcing his safe arriVal at Kimberley, and asking " What won the Oaks ?''

A Dundee Cerrespondent sayS that influenza has broken eat in DalmoraPeastle,,and a number of the servants are suffering from tthe malady. Her Majesty, in order to avoid the -cold evening winds at present soprevalent, is driving out earlier in the afternoon than usual.

Lord George Hamilton has at last started off on his journey, but he .rs still very weak and has had a most serious attack of influrAza, and at one time was in great danger. Lord Knutsford has re- covered badly, and has not got up his strength, but he attends to business.

Leon being4t ,member of the Jewish faith, was in some fliffionity wheii, on Monday morning, he.approached the table of the House of Commons to take the-oath. As is well known; Jews take the 'oatt with their 'beads covered. Mr. Leon adroitly compromised ,by ,holding ,his hat over his head (without actually placing it on his brows) whilst the oath was administered to him.

The diTe:ctors -ef the company which has been fformed to erect an " Eiffel Tower at Blackpool 'have metin ,London to make a selection from the large number of •designs submitted. After a pro- longed consideration the ..plans sent in by Messrs. , Maxwell and Take, of Manchester, were adopted. I mnderstand that the arrangements for carrying out tile project are in •a' forward state.

To carry on the Welsh Disestablishment campaign it he Campaign• Committee has addressed an appeal to the Nonconformistt and Liberals of the Paincipa- 4ity, and to Welshmen and Liberals everywhere, for s sum of not Jess than... Z-10,000. The Welsh National Council has decided to carry on in the English con- stituencies a ',vigorous effort to lay before the elec- tors the case of Wales' for Disestablishment and Dis- iendowsoent.

It is exceedingly probable that the Duke of Edinburgh Will resign the command at Devonport in the course of a few,montbs, because the Duchess cannot be induced td live there. She was strongly opposed to this acceptance of , this post, and posi- tively refuses to'bury I:herself at Devonport. The Duchess and therdaughters are coming to England shortly, but her ,stay at iDevonpert will be limited to a very few weeks, and she is going back to Germany:at thetnd Of July.

The fdllowing story Of the late ,Archbishop of York has been sent tome. I should be very sorry to answer for its authenticity, for it has somewhat the ring of the Joe Miller epoch. But as I never heard it before myself, it will. probably-be new to some of my readers-:—" 'After.his severe illness a few years ego Bishop Magee k was ordered away for " change and rest:" "The landlord of the hotel at which he stayed brought/ him the visitors' book be- fore he left. with a special vpquest that he would contribute a few 'remarks. IThel3ishop wrote: "I came here for .change and rest. ' The waiters got the change. The landlord.got the rest." •

ACROSS THE ATLANTIC (No. 3) HOW IT STRIKES THE STRANGER. BY " TOWNSMAN:: . Brilliant sunshine favoured our 'first view of American soil, and the weather was very pleasant as we set foot on the Hub of the Universe. Boston is a second Liverpool. It occupies an irregular position at the mouth of the Charles river, a fine waterway which is always crowded with shipping. It does an immense coasting and export trade for the manufacturing cities of Massachusetts, and all the wealth of New England seems to 'flow through it. It embraces a population of about hallo million, which in the poorer -quarters cC the city is cooped in a very confined area. In the words of residents, its streets follow the " way Use cows went to pas- ture," and they deviate with the variew of an old English town. The business portion is wery exten- sive and spreads over half the city. A4peculiar but time-saving feature is that all the houses of a trade are close together, and this arrangement is carried out to such an extent that even a dozen doctors will occupy rooms on the samelat. Some of the busi- ness premises are palatial structures, and tower to great heights. Buildings of nine storeys are very common, and occasionally some rise to ten and twelve, while a very conspicuous block in Washing- ton-st rises to at storeys, and would have been higher but for the interference of the authorities. It is a noble erection in white stone, and most. of the edifices are either of stone -or faced bricks dressed with stone. To reach the top of these places recourse is had to elevators, which are kept on the move from early morn to late in the evening, and in some instances it is doubtful whether they are ever still. THE STREETS, (OVERHEAD Aro/RES, &C. From an English .point of view the streets are simply hideous. The footpaths are freely decorated with posts of various kinds and purposes, from huge telegraph posts of all shapes-+apparently forest trees just stripped of their bark, and carrying cross- bars that cannot approach an English telegraph pole , for symmetry —to small iron pillars to carry electric wires. In the main streets, the thorough- fares are simply a-close network of overhead wires —wires telegraphic, telephonic,- electric-wires for lighting the streets-and for running the tram cars. Then the rails the latter sun upon are such that no English Corporation could tolerate. They are clumsy in the extreme, and it is ,no unusual thing to see a cart that attempts to cross them slide along , for half a dozen yards before it can get over. The rails are inches above the pavement of the streets, , and if adopted in 'Manchester would soon put an , end to the pirate "busses running along the lines. , The road pavement is mostly of stone so irregularly laid as to be eminently calculated to shatter the stoutest built vehicle, and as a consequence all the conveyances are ,liberally supplied with springs. The street cleansing is carried out in a frightful manner, and clouds of dust float-down the avenues with the least wind, blinding -every person on the streets and filling-his clothes with a fine powder. So abominable is the paving that it is impossible to run a street brushing-machine, and men have to brush down the nicks the narrow-way of the streets instead of along its length. THR tSHOPS AND tOBTICES. There is nothing enticing about a Boston shop. No attempt is made at windowedressing, the goods being apparently thrown in haphazard on a flat window bottom, and tickets tacked on them. As a rule, the shop winnows are wery small, and the shops themselves long and narrow, extending across a block, with doors in two streets. The prettiest shops in the city are the florists' which are ablaze with fre-h spring glowers, that -give to them a very refreshing appearance, and that attract hosts of sightseers. Here, as elsewhere, the drapers have the largest business premises and many of them are said to be very wealthy. Certainly if their ad- vertisements in the local journals are any criterion of their trade, they must be doing .a great amount of business. But the life of a -draper's assistant is not an enviable one. We met on the street one day a young Londoner who was engaged in it "dry goods store," and who was taking -a three weeks vacation on the streets. He told ns.the." drive" in the stores was frightful, and the assistants were not permitted to rest for a minute. He was so dis.; satisfied that he had thrice attempted to.stow him- self away on a homeward bound ,shp-but in vain, and he was now submitting to the inevitable. The offices, on the other hand, do not --seem to work their servants hard. From what we saw of clerks, we were forced to the conclusion that they took life very easily, and in many cases-it appeared that their hardest work was to kill time. .The offices are luxuriously furnished, and everything that can add to the enjo Jment of life and promote the saving of labour is obtained. Type writers are4verywhere,and we were informed that the time is not far distant when the newspapers will refuse to take any but typewritten "copy." How your compositors would rejoice at that prospect ! Mr. Henry T. P. Bates, correspondent, Boston Herald," Boston, Mass, furnished me with the following unsolicited testi- monial of the Caligraph machine—" This is a sample of the work that the Caligraph will do, and I con- sider that it is the best machine for newspaper work ' that has yet been invented. If you should ever find the necessity of using a writing machine of any kind I should most certainly advise you to procure a Caligraph. •It is, of course, every man-for his own horse. I think that this is the best; men who use Remington machines consider that one the beste and just the same with all the different ones. I have used three different ones, and I can get better speed and more correct work on this than any other kind that I have ever tried." WHAT AMERICANS EAT. Perhapsthe greatest change an Englishman finds in America is in thefeeding habits of the people. There is nothing substantial about their food. They delight in an" infinite variety," and they take the most astonish- ing combinations. tlt is no wonder the Americans are a pale faced, restless race, and that dentists and doctors liflourish. They take their meals hot with bread fresh from the oven, and-wash them down with hot drinks, ~of which there is -a. great number. The latter are mostly I.chemical concoctions,, and are obtained from druggists, -whose chief businers it.is apparently to supply. drinks. For the edification ,of, your readers I give a bill-of fare from a very flourishing restaurant in Washington street, tree heart of the city, on-Friday, May Ist :

THE ELAiIED BIHTISHER.

We gathered very early that the best hated immi- grant was the Britisher. This is owing to the fact that all the principal positions in American politics are con- trolled by the Irish and the Catholics. "There's no chance here for a man unless he's a Catholic" greeted us continually in our intercourse with all sorts of people, "The Catholics control everything." So glaring has this fact become that three years ago the Englishmen in Massachusetts organised themselves and founded a society called" The British American Citizen" in con- nection with which they publish& weekly newspaper, The Society numbers some 70,000 members,but the great ! complaint is that directly the English get to the States they cease to take any interest in politics. The Irish, on the other hand, take naturally to politics, and have thus obtained an ascendency. At the last election, however, the society nearly changed the representation 111 the

div.head: 'ANOTHER FIGHT FOR FREBDOBT.
div.p: 'ANOTHER FIGHT FOR FREBDOBT.

Of course we visited Bunkers Hill, and saw the spOt where the!first blow was struck for American indepen- dence. 'his a pretty place and is new marked by a per- fectly plain monument, another memorial a little further away recording the names of the local men and officers who fell in the encounter. There is also a life-sized statue of Colonel Prescott who led the dissatisfied Colonists. Whilst in Boston we heard frequent references to the " Coming fight," and our curiosity being excited we ap- pea.led,to a shrewd old Scotchman who has been long in the country. "It's singular," said he "how many wars have been fought on so-called religious grounds, when there-wasn't a particle of religion in them. We are bound to have a religious war here sooneror later. It isToming slowly but surely, and it will be between the Catholics and the Protestants for the possession of the Continent. It will be another fight for freedom. Whenever the Catholics are kept in their place they are as agreeable as can be, but directly they get a little power they show a disposition to perpetuate the practices of the middle ages. It is part of their system. The Church of Rome is ever the same." This opinion was strongly confirmed a few days later, when I read in the "New York Tribune," the following :—" The Catholic Review," of this city urges that Roman Catholic delegates from all the countries of Latin America be invited to attend the great Catholic Congress which is to be held in Chicago during the session of the World's Fair in 1883. In some 'of these countries it says the church has lost its prestige, and even the more intelligent classes cannot have much respect for the faith. But if they saw the strength of Catholicism in this country, their interest in it would be revived "The destinies of this Continent," says" The Review," "are particularly in Catholic hands. We are strongly in- terested in the United States and Canada., and our owner- ship of the Continent from the Rio Grande to Cape Horn is undisputed. Only themost criminal neglect and indif- ference on the part of the bishops, the clergy, and the leaders of the laity can lose to us this magnificent heri- tage:" Thus the aim of the Romish Church for territorial aggrandisement is made plain. SHALL DRINKERS STAN", ?

A question that agitates the the State of Masiachusetts stands above. The drinking saloons, as the firs-water dens are called, are more like English wine shops than public-houses. In the windows are arranged a number of bottles, and in the shops small tables with seats are placed down each side. The saloon keepers are taxed to the tune of $l,OOO (£200) and upwards for their licenses, the money being appropriated for several purposes,such as educatien, street repairs, &c. On Sundays and holi- days the bars are rigidly closed. But it seems the native American does not take kindly to the new regulation as to sitting down to his drinks. He likes to go into a saloon, give his order at the bar, drink his liquor and be gone. But the State law says he shall walk in, take a seat, give his order toa waiter, and drink his grog where he sits. This, say some, is a direcst encouragement to drinking habits, and strong opposition is manifested to the regulation. The heavy tax is regarded as quite right and proper, but why should drinkers be compelled to sit ? So far no satisfactory reply has been given to the query.

div.head: .A:XERICAN WOMEN.
div.p: .A:XERICAN WOMEN.

Another strange feature in American life is the large number of women engaged in business. Go where you will, you,will find women engaged in some capacity or other. They edit newspapers,collect news,act as clerks, cashiers' and book-keepers ; n d ecoupy many positions usualiy filled by men at home. They are usually fairly tall, slimly built, and, to my mind, thinly attired. Their dresses hang about them in a very • peculiar manner, as they rush along with the gait dinen. They have the same sallow complexion as their.brothers, and are any- thing but pretty. As .a rule, they are deficient in the minor matters of commercial education,but theymanage to get along. Colleges to train young ladies for business life are fairly numerous, and their prices are quite stiff. I would not mind runnine, a college at half the rates charged. When. they profess to teach shorthand in 13 lessons, it is no wonder if they teach other subjects as quickly,that the ladies are not thoroughly versed in office work. But there is a disposition to try them, and some of the ladies must make a good 'living in reasonable hours,and in congenial labour.

div.head: LOCAL PREACHER'S EXPERIENCE.
div.p: A LOCAL PREACHER'S EXPERIENCE.

One day in November, 1886, Mr. William Cruick- shank was attending in a public meeting in Willington, near Durham. In this mere fact there is nothing important, but in what 'befell him at the meeting, there is.

He lately told the story himself as follows. First, , however, itsmust be understood that Mr. Cruickshank is a local preacher. Now a local preacher is a brother licensed in the Methodist Episcopal Church, the Wesleyan 'Methodist Church, and other branches of that great denomination, to preach the Gospel without being the regular pastor of a congregation. Heearns his living in -any way he likes, and preaches when.called upon. The local preachers are a useful-and zealousbody of men. With this preface on our ,part, we will let Mr. Cruickshank relate his experience. He says: "While at the Willington meeting something suddenly seized me. My left hand fell down by my side, and as often as I raised it, it fell again. A strange feeling came over me, and I went out to get the fresh air to see if it would revive me. I reeled like a drunken man, and felt excited and tremulous, as if I was going out of my .mind. As best I could I dragged on towards my home, tbut was afraid of people seeing me, lest they should thinlyl was ,in drink. With great difficulty I reached home, but had not the power to open-the door. A friend, seeing-my trouble, came and helped me into the house. , A doctor was sent for, but said little or nothing as to the cause of -my seizure. I got no relief from his medicine, and far. days I was not able to dress myself, and had to keep in, the house." This, briefly, stated, is what happened at the meeting and immediately after it. But what was the matter? To answer this question we must hear Mr. Cruicashank a little further. Ile goes on to say: "Off and on I have suffered for thirty years from indigestion and stomach complaint. I always had a bad taste in my mouth, especially in the morning and often hap to go to my work in the coal-mine without touching food. I could scarcely eat anything without having great pain after it, and grew so badithat I often had to leave my work for a day or two at a time. Now I would be better, now worse, but never well. What I suffered tongue cannot tell. Later on I was taken with sciatica and pains in the hip and groin, from which I suffered dreadfully. For weeks I could not bear the weight of my foot, and when in bed had to have my leg swung so as to give me rest." At this point in Mr. Cruickshank's story •comes in the incident already ;related—the seizure at the meeting.

Then he adds: From this tinae (November, 186)I felt very weak; my legs would shake, and I trembled all over. There was a sinking, weak, sickly feeling at the pit of my stomach, with great fulness as if the stomach ,wene swelled or blown out. Every kind of herb or medi- cine that I could hear of I tried, but received very little benefit. In November, 1888, I got a book telling of a medicine called Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and I made up my mind to try it. So I procured a bottle from Mr. Elliott's, the grocer in Willington, and after taking the first bottle I felt much better and stronger, and after taking four bottles I WEaS cured. All the pain completely left me, ad I have never ailed anything since. lam a local preacher, and before taking the Syrup could only fill appointments near home, but now' I can go anywhere, and recently I walked five miles with ease, notwithstand- lam seventy-seven years of age. You are at liberty to publish my statement, and to say I will answer the in- quiries of other sufferers about my case. "WILLIAM CRINCICSHANJE, 11, Commercial Street, Willington, near Durham."

In the light of these facts, the nature of the seizure at the meeting is as plain as can be. It was paralysis, which might have crippled him for life, or proved fatal on the spot.,.. It was caused by bile acids in the blood, which- are the products of indigestion and dyspepsia, of which Mr. C. had so long been a victim. More than 90 per cent. of the nervous disorders of people of every age are due to the stomach and liver— indigestion and dyspepsia. Mother Seigel's Syrup thoroughly cured this, and thus gave our good friend the local preacher a fresh leise of life and power to con- tinue his praiseworthy work. •

ALCOHOLICS IN INFLUENZA.

In reply to inquiries by the Alliance Press Agency as to his hospital and private treatment of influenza, Dr. Edmunds, the Senior Physician to the London Temperance Hospital, writes as follows :—" We have had quite as influx of very serious hang cases of an adynamic and unusual type—cases which we regard as instances of the most fatal forms of the prevailing epidemic. In the treatment of these we have entirely abstained from the prescription of alcoholics, and considering the nature of the cases, we are more than satisfied with the results of treat- ment on classical lines, apart altogether from the use of alcohol. Among my private patients I have had several well-known public men suffering from influenza, with the dangerous lung complications. -None of these have been treated with alcohol, and they have all recovered most favourably, one of these patients being Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., who had excruciating neuralgia in the head, in addition to severe febrile disease and lung complications, and who is now convalescing admirably. What I prescribe is absolute rest in bed, careful nutrition at frequent intervals, and especially so in persons of spare habit, who I find run down very rapidly. As medicines 1 give a mild fever mixture of citrate of ammonia and henbane, and, on the abatement of fever, I follow up with quinine. In the neuralgia cases I stop the sufferings by beginning with' one or two 20-grain doses of quinine and a subcutaneous injection of 4to 5-10ths of a grain of morphia. In the nutrition I attach much importance to carefully made beef-tea and milk gruel, with barley water acidulated with fresh lemon juice as a .drink while the febrile thirst continues. I ought not to shrink from adding that I believe the mortality of these cases has been largely due to the craze for adminis- tering alcohol—a craze which those who are inter- ested in the sale of alcoholic beverages take every opportunity of stimulating."
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr. Balharry presided, and there were also present Messrs. Heaton; Davies, D. Jones Dobson, Aukland, Mather, Hood-Wright, W. Houghton, J. Houghton, Smith, Gill, Humphreys, Turton, Jolley, Mather, Hibbert ; J. C. Sutton (clerk), S. Sutton (Assistant clerk), C. H. Ward (Workhouse master), and H. M. Mines (superintendent of Padgate Schools).
THB SCHOOLS.-RESIGNATIONS AND THB CAUSE THEREOF,

The Schools Committee recommended that the tender of Mr. Josiah Whittle, of Warrington, be accepted for painting and decorating the committee room and two other rooms for the sum of £l2. The assistant school- master, Mr. Bailey, and the foster-mother,Miss Dearden, tendered their resignations of their respective appoint- ments which the committee recommended to be accepted. Mr. W. Houghton, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, said the resignation of the assistant school- master was due to the fact that he had obtained a better situation, while Miss Dearden resigned because, he be- lieved, she was going to be married to the assistant master. (Laughter.)

div.head: THB HODBL.
div.p: THB HODBL.

The House Committee reported that the application of Mr. W. Owen, secretary of the School of Art, for a work- house inmate, named John Simpson, to sit as a " model " at the School of Art at a shilling per sitting, was acceded to, and it was decided that the money be paid to the treasurer.—Confirmed.

TIM INFLUENZA. In answer to a question, Mr. Ward said there were 16 cases of influenza in the Workhouse hospital, but there had been no deaths. The Clerk said that Mr. Harbourne's (the relieving officers) expenses were larger than usual just now and it appeared that this was due to the fact that there was at present a larger amount of sickness to be provided for, owing chiefly to the influenza. Mr. Mines said there was none of the children at Padgate Schools suffering from the malady.

SPIRITUAL PROVISION FOR 'INMATES. A letter was read from the Rev. J. Ingham Brook, arch- deacon of Halifax, asking the Board's co-operation with the Committee appointed at the last session of the York, convocation to inquire into the spiritual provision made for the inmates of Workhouses within the province of York, and enclosing a number of questions to which an- swers were invited. From the answers to these inquiries which had been filled in by the Workhouse master, it appeared that there were 300 inmates in the Workhouse ; 'l6O children at Padgate over five years of age ; and 46 in the Workhouse mostly under five years of age. There was at . the Workhouse a chaplain recognised by the Local Government Board and paid quarterly a salary of £5O iper annum. There was a service and sermon on Sunday afternoons in the Workhouse dining hall. About five hours per week was spent by the chaplain in visiting the wards and Infirmary. The wards were visited regularly by others than the chaplain, but no special arrangements were made for such visits. Holy communion was not celebrated in the Workhouse except in extreme cases of illness; others were allowed to go to the church when the chaplain requested. The children over five years were only in the Workhouse 14 days and then passed on to Padgate Schools. Seven of the officers at the Work- house belonged to the Church of England and three were Presbyterians. This was all the business.

div.head: TEMPORARY V YRNWY PIPE LINK
div.p: THE TEMPORARY V YRNWY PIPE LINK
CROSSING THE lIERSEY.

The temporary pipe line conveying the Vyrnwy water supply to Liverpool is now approaching com- pletion, and when the finishing touches have been successfully given, the householders of Liverpool will soon be in possessson of the long-talked-of 'water supply. The Norton Tower, on the Cheshire , side of the river, was successfully filled with water ' some few weeks ago, and the pipes were charged with water down to the Cheshire bank of the river Mersey, at a point two miles from Widnes and four from Warrington. Further than this, however, it could not go until the temporary pipe line across the Mersey had been placed in position. It trans- pired that, preliminary arrangements had been com- pleted, and that an attempt would be made to lay the pipe in position at Sunday morning's tide. At 3:30 on Sunday morning the only indication of in- tended operations was the arrival of six horses from the stables of Mr. Pilkington. contractor. Warring- ton, which had been engaged to be on the spot at 4 a.m., to assist in the work. The pipe is composed of 50 sections of 12-inch steel flexible tubes. The entire length of 800 feet of the pipe was sunk in a trench and set on wooden rails resting on the ground, such as are used to take barrels off lurries. Along each side, and extending the •entire length of the pipe and passing through each of these blocks of wood, was a strong wire rope. These two ropes were firmly secured at the extreme end of the pipe from the river, and extended across the river to the Cheshire side, where they were fastened to a steam winch, the intention evidently being to wind the rope round the steam winch, and thus pull the long heavy pipe across the water where it would sink into position. The trench from about 200 feet from the edge of the water formed a comparatively steep slope. There were eight boats moored across the river at regular distances, with the object of guiding the line of the pipe. The pipe is 12in. in diameter, but the temporary pipe line from Norton Tower to the river,and again from the river to Liverpool, is 18in. Norton Tower is about 3001 t. above the river, from which it is distant two miles. This will give the water an enormous impetus through that 12in. pipe in the river,so great that it is estimated the 5,000,000 gallons of water per day will be supplied by this means to Liverpool.

At Seven a.m. the first movements were made towards getting the tackling in order. The number of workmen rapidly increased, and soon set to work to have all in readiness for the evening tide. At five o'clock in the afternoon a large number of visitors had assembled, and these and the officials watched the rising of the tide, the former with interest and the latter with anxiety. It was high water a little after six, and at 5.50 the horses were attached at the end of the pipes furthest from the river, and steam was got up on the Cheshire side. The concluding operations were as successful as those of drawing the pipe across the water. The exact time of drawing the pipe across the river—that is, not includ- ing the time occupied in making the trial pulls to see if the pipe was in a perfect working order, and again wait- ing for the highest water mark when the pipe was in the, mid-river—was 27i minutes. When the pipe was drawn up on the Cheshire side, the plugs which closed the end of the pipe as it was being taken , across were removed,. and a temporary connection made with the pipe containing the Vyrnwy water from Norton Tower. The plugs in the Lancashire end of the pipe were also removed, and within an hour from the start of the launch of the pipe Vyrnwy water flowed through the pipe across the river, and discharged itself in the trench on the Lancashire side,the accomplishment of this long-desired feat bAng greeted with "Three Cheers for the Vyrnwy Water." The officials and all the . workmen, as well as the spectators, were pleasantly sur- prised at the complete success of so difficult an under- taking. Owing to the great strength of the current, the greatest precautions had to be adopted, but all the diffi- culties were successfully overcome.

During Sunday night and Monday the pipe was gra- dually working itself into its proper position. The flexible joints of the pipe worked so successfully that on Monday morning the whole pipe was below the bottom of the channel. The sections were all sounded on Monday,and found perfectly in order. Navigation, which has been delayed, owing to the nature of the tides, was resumed on Tuesday, and no interruption or damage of any kind whatever is anticipated from the sunken pipe. It was owing to the nature of the neap tide that• Sunday was chosen for the launch, that day's tide being the most suitable that could have been available for some days to come.
PERCIVAL GORDON;
OR, THE CHILD OF THE REGIMENT.

div.head: BY SYLVANUS COBB.
div.p: BY SYLVANUS COBB.
CHAPTER XIV. OLD TOM'S MISFORTONE.S.

On the morning of the day on which Tom Craw- ford was expected to arrive at Wenham the earl called Percival into his study, remarking that he had something of importance to communicate. "May I hope, my lord," said the youth, "that you will tell me why you have been so downcast since the arrival of yesterday morning's mail? and may the telling give you relief." "Dear boy, to tell you the cause of my sadness is the purpose for which I have called you. I had thought that I would not speuk,—that I would leave Old TOM to tell the story himself, as he expects to do. But,—dear old soul !—I will relieve him so far as that. He shall not be obliged to smite you without warning. Yet,—bear this in mind,—There is room for hope. I hardly know how to—"

"Hold 1" interrupted Percival, putting forth his hand. He had, in the outset, trembled, and turned pale; but he had put away the emotion, and now looked up with a smile. "I think I eau speak for you. You have to tell me that my family papers are lost?" "They are missing, dear Percival. Tom writes to me, in his letter, the principal facts. When I so pleasantly hailed you, in the breakfast room, I had only read the opening paragraph of the missive. The papers have been stolen; and Tom thinks he knows the thief." "But who could wish to steal them? Of what value can they be to any one else ? " "You forget, my dear boy, that they are your only proof of heirship to Ambleton. Without them you could never hope to claim the name, even, of your father's family; for you will remember that your father bore another name in the army, as did you., "But," said the youth, "if I remember rightly my father had my name entered in the Register of Saint Anthony's as GORDON; and he so gave it to the clerk of the district." "Aye," responded the general, with a faint smile • "but the record of tact might destroy all that if we cannot produce the direct and indisput- able evidence contained in those papers." "I see; I see. Certainly the loss will leave me as simple son of Robert and Bessie Coverley." "Of course. But we must wait until we see Tom. He can tell us more; and he may have learned more since he wrote. You are not sorry I told you ? " " Sorry ! My lord, I thank you a thousand times. I should have pitied poor Tom had it been his to break the news to me. As it is, I should have ceased to care for it when he arrives. I mean, I shall not mourn. nf course, I hope the papers slay be recovered; and to that end we will hope." In the afternoon of that day Tom Crawford arrived; a hale, hearty, handsome man, of four.- and fifty, seemingly as young as ever, save one lame arm—the lett,—the shoulder of which had been shot through by a musket-ball, at Talavera. "Come, come, dear old Tom," cried Percival, seeing how down-hearted the poor fellow was, and knowing well the cause,—" you must put on your smiles for dinner. The general has told me all about the papers, and I have not one thought of blame for you. After dinner, over your pipe and a glass of grog, you shall tell us the whole story." So, pretty soon, Tom's face was smiling, as of old, and the dinner passed pleasantly. In the evening, sitting in the library, the old sergeant told the story of the loss. Said he: . .

"I have in my room a good strong desk, with a firm, excellent lock, furnished by government, in which to keep blanks, and duplicate reports,—or, rather, my retained copy of triplicates. In the same room with me has been an old ordnance clerk, named Felix McAllister,—a man sixty yea cs old, at least, badly wounded at Waterloo, and in the arsenal since his discharge from hospital. I had liked him, and made a chum of him, and one evening, feeling in the mood,—feeling that I iniv.t talk to somebody about my brave boy,—l told him of Percival Gordon; and perhaps I told him more than 1 ought. We had a bottle of rum,—we always kept a bottle that we bought in common,— he one time, and I the next,—we sipped from that, and smoked, and my tongue was free. Wnen began to tell of my hero, I didn't know where to stop. "However, when I had told all I cared to tell; McAllister asked about the boy's parentage, and X, ;mond of the opportunity, told of Captain Archy Gordon, son of Sir Timothy, of Gordoneroft, and of the grandmother, on the sane side. I noticed that when I came to speak of Sir William Patten, of Ambleton, he was interested; but, I thought, only because the lad should have come from two titled families. He wasn't inquisitive, at all,—and there was no need; for I told him all there was to tell about the Patten family, so far as you, dear boy, were concerned. It was all of a month ago that we held this conversation.

"Just a week ago McAllister received leave of absence, to be gone through the summer months. His chief had gone to Italy, and there was nothing for him to do. Four days ago, when I b,gan to arrange for this visit, one of the first things I thought of was your packet of papers. I went to my desk, looked where I had left it, and found it—gone I Nothing else had been dist.,rbed. As soon as I could collect my senses, and think clearly, I made a thorough search, but to no avail. The papers were gone—had been stolen, I knew.

"It flashed upon me in a moment that McAllister was the thief. He was the only man, besides my- self, who knew where they were. One evening, as we sat together, I had occasion to move the packet, to get a bit of paper that lay beneath it, and as I laid it on top of the desk for a moment he saw it, and being attracted by its seals, and its evident age, he asked me what it was. I answered him without hesitation, simply the truth. Said I, They are papers belonging to my dear ward—my hero of a hundred battles l' And as spoke, I put the packet back in place, and locked the desk.

"As far as his being able to steal the papers was concerned, it was the easiest thing in the world for him to do. He had but to get up while I was asleep, take my keys from my pocket, and open my desk, and I know very well that he did it.

"All I knew of his home was, that he belonged somewhere in the South of England—he had always given me to understand, in Sussex. When I went to the office of the commandant, however, they told me he had gone down into Devonshire, but they didn't know to what part. When I get ready to look for him, I shall make my first visit to Ambleton, for I can't help thinking, since this thing turned up, that he has some interest in some shape, in the family affairs of the Pattens. Do you know, General, where the place is ? " "Certainly, and know the present baronet, Sir Edward Patten. Ambleton is not more than twenty miles distant, in a north-westerly direction, about half way between Exeter and Tiverton." "I hope I shall find my man there. 0! I shall be careful, never fear. If he's got the papers—and I know he has—l shall get them back, be sure. And now, tell me—You don't think me much to blame do you 7"
"Dear old Tom ! " cried our hero, with generous impulse, "don't you borrow one bit of trouble on that score. Certainly, I cauuot see that you are to blame in the least.

"No," said the earl, to whom both the others looked for his opinion. "If there is any blame it must rest with me. I ought to have had fore- thought enough—or, in plain language, sense enough to have put papers of so much importance in the keeping of my banker. In his safety vault they would have been surely. safe. However, the deed has been done, and we must hope that the thief may be found." And there the matter was permitted to rest for the night. On the following day, Old Tom, who could not rest until he had put forth an effort, took one of Wenham's horses—a splendid roadster—and made his way to Ambleton, Percival bearing him com- pany, for the latter had a strong desire to see the place in question—the place on which his mother's grandfather had reigned as lord of the manor, I where her father was born and reared, and where her aged uncle was present master. The place was found without difficulty, and a fine old place it was. There was a single street, extending from a beautiful vale up the side of a gently sloping hill, with an old Gothic church, of Portland stone, at the lower end, while the broad park of the Hall faced the upper end. The dis- tance between the two points was little less than a mile, wherein lay a pretty village, with a good inn, and shops of all kinds. A broad sweep of land, I beautifully broken into hill and dale, meadow and woodland, was divided into outlying farms, and the whole property—village, and farms, and adjacent quarries of stone—belonged .to the baronet who occupied the great Hall on the hillside—Ambleton

• Hair called Uy some, and by others, Andsleton Abbey, because once an abbey had occupied a site where now stood one of Sir Edward's large barns. The rent roll was very large—Lord Wenham after- wards told them it was very nearly as large as his own. But Felix McAllister they did not find, though they were upon his track. Percival remained in the background, allowing Tom to do all the search- ing. McAllister had been at the ion, and had remained there three nights, spending his days in looking over the place. Tom told the landlord that he and Felix were room-mates and chums at Woolwich, that he had heard that his old friend was in the place, and he had hoped to find him. Then he asked if _Felix had ever lived in that neighbourhood. "Why, bless you !" Boniface replied heartily. "us old father was butler at the Hall in Sir William's time ; and Felix began there. He was a boy in the stables till he was well-growd, and then he went with the master of the hounds; but the life didn't suit him. He wanted to be a soldier, and a soldier he became. He went off and 'listed, and from that time he's only been back here two or three times. His father died while he was in Spain, fighting the French. And he fought the same French again at Waterloo; and there he was wounded; and I do believe he hasn't had any fighting to do since." Tom learned from the good-natured landlord that Felix would certainly be back again, because he had said he should spend a month at the inn and at the Hall, at any rate. With regard to the direction he had taken, the host could only say that he had gone towards Exeter, and from there he thought he would go over into Dorchester. And, with this intelligence, and a very fair look at the estate of Ambleton, the old sergeant and the young captain set out on their return to Wen- ham. When they had reported to the earl he took the matter up with zeal. "We will suppose," he said, "that the masa McAllister has the papers." "My lord," put in Tom, with decided emphasis,, ; "I've thought the matter all ovdr, and all through, and you can set it down as is fixed fact that Felix McAllister has got our boy's papers." "All right," nodded Wenham. "We will con- sider that as settled. And now, what did he want. ,of them? To me the matter is plain. This man j McAllister was born and reared on the Manor of I Ambleton, and, naturally, he feels an interest in I all that concerns the family of its lord. He knows I that the present baronet, whom he served in his early youth, is near to his end, and that he must die leaving no child, or near relative, to succeed him. With this on his mind, McAllister hears your story of our young hero, and learns from you that , his grandmother, on his father's side, was a certain Mary Patten, daughter of a certain George Patten, and that said George Patten's father was Sir William Patten, baronet, of Ambleton. All this you, Tom, told him, freely and unreservedly. "Beyond this he can read and understand for himself, for he knows the family history. He knows that George Patten was a younger brother, that an elder brother, Charles, succeeded to the title, and that the son of Charles came next in succession, leaving the progeny of George out in the cold, for the then present, at least. He knows, further, that the present lord of the manor, Sir Edward, was the only son and only child of that elder brother, Sir Charles and that, in the event of Sir Edward's death without issue, the issue of George came to the front; and, further, the youth of wbom he has been told, is the only direct lineal descendant of said George Patten. "Then McAllister learns about those • papers, and naturally enough, from what he is told, he judges them to be of family matters. "And now we come to the man's motive in the theft. If those papers are what he thinks, he may, if he can possess them, turn them to golden account. In one respect, he will be master of the situation, and may, he fancies, command his own price. Very likely, somewhere, there is another party who might present legal claim to this succession ; and if he be a man of means, he may be open to a good bargain. Or, should he be a poor man, with • those papers in his possession he might gain the estate, and pay to his helper a goodly sum sub- sequently. "So, my friends, I look upon the matter; and now, Tom, it remains with you to find the fellow, and force him to disgorge. I think you will have no trouble beyond finding him—that is, if you find him before he has disposed of his prize. And here let me give you a hint. Meet him, if you can, before he returns to Ambleton. Should he see the host of the Ambleton Aims, he would' learn of your visit, and might be on his guard; whereas, if you take hi— unawares, you will have the advantago." The matter was further discussed; and, in the end, it was arranged that Tom should set forth at once, and commence his search for the thief. He would go first t. Exeter, and he believed he should be able to find a trace of his man either there or on the roads running eastward, as the landlord at Ambleton had said he was going into Dorset- shire. Let Us now turn oace more to the Earl of Elm- dale and his daughter. The ride home was taken in comparative silence, both parent and child given up to thoughts w hich they were not prepared to speak. But Richard Archer could not retire with the heavy burden upon his mind. Late in the evening, after tea had been served, as he and his daughter. sat together in the library, he arose and closed half open door, after which he took a seat near the stand at which the maiden was reading; and she knew, as she saw the movement, wl.at was coming. For the moment her heart throbbed painfully ; but she had been expecting the ordeal and was, prepared to meet it. Yet the earl was the most deeply perplexed of the two. He picked up a. paper and laid it down; then handled a paper- knife until ..his thoughts were in fit control for. speech.
" Caroline," he said, with an effort, "I have a word to say to you—an important word—and I trust you will be frank with me, and—and"

As he father's courage failed, the courage of the daughter came to the surface. She saw how he suffered, and in pity she came to his aid. "Dear papa," she said, looking up into his face with affectionate sweetness, "I know what you would say, and I have a mind to help you out. You wish to speak of Percival Gordon. You know that _I love him, and that he loves me."

"No, no, my child," the earl interrupted, "Say not so. 1 have feared that you might learn to love him if you did not take heed in season." "0, papa! you cannot so deceive yourself. You know that I love him. You know that I have loved him since that terrible night on which he. saved me from a dreadful death. When we were but little children we plighted our troth and solemnly pledged our faith to one another. Perci- val, in that long-gone time, sitting in a vine-clad arbour at Salvaterra, promised me that, when he should have become a captain in the army, he would come and claim me for his own; and I promised him that I would wait for him. And I have waited for him.

" You, papa, affianced me to Matthew Egerton. You did not ask me to consent; you did not con- sult me in any way ; only, after you had done the deed, you asked me how, when I should have grown to be a lady, I should like that boy for my husband. You surely remember my answer. You remember that the thought horrified me; and from that time to this you have never again spoken to me directly upon the subject. Now, papa, let me have done with Matthew Egerton." She drew her- self proudly up; her eyes were aglow with indig- nant flame; and every feature was fixed in firm resolution.

"I loathe and despise him," she said, with her hands tightly clenched. "He is unworthy to be your son-in-law. The union would disgrace you, while it made me unutterably miserable. I know that, were you to force the union, the time would come when you would repent it in sackcloth and ashes.

"Father, I cannot speak the name of my own true lover in the same breath that has uttered the name of Matthew Egerton. Let this matter rest for now. Let us both think and reason, and take counsel with our own true hearts; and at another time we will speak of him whose presence has Overt you so much disquiet. " Papa I dear papa! will you excuse me for the present? I have no heart to speak further on this subject. By and by, when lam calm and in the mood, I will come to you of my own accord, and we will talk freely and frankly.' "Go, my child," the earl cried, laying his hand upon his daughter's head, "and may God blesi and keep you, and all good angels guard and guide you." lie kissed her, seeming glad thus to close the unhappy scene. It might be only postponing the evil to another time ; but he felt that he could rest, with the ice only broken, much botter tnan with subiect unbroached, as it was before. - (To be c.:fltlinueti).

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. _ _
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. _ _

HOUSE OF LORDS.—M ONDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at half-past four. BILLS ADVANCED.—The Local Government (Ireland) Provisional Order (No. 1) Bill passed through Committee. The report of amendments to the Pier and Harbour Provisional Orders (No. 1) Bill was received and agreed to.

The House adjourned at 4.35. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAY. The Speaker took the chair at seven minutes past three. VOLUNTEER Lo.e.a.—The SECRETARY of ST ATE for WAR, in answer to a question, said he would carefully oonsider the advisibility of introducing a Bill to'authorise I 1 e Public Works Loan Commissioners to grant loans for volunteer drill halls on the same easy terms as were given for other public works. PARCELS POST TO THE UNITED STATES. The POST- VASTER-GENERAL informed Mr. Henniker Heaton that sue of his first official acts had been to proposethe estab- lishment of a parcels post between this country and the United States, and he had sinee lost no opportunity of Urging the advantage that must accrue.; up to the pre- Sent, however, without success. MAJOR GRANT'S NATI VENROOPS.—Replying to Viscount Curzon, Sir JOHN GORST stated that the gallant services of the native troops serving under Major Grant in Mani- Pur would be suitably recognised. ETHER AS A POISON.—The CHANCELLOR of the Ex- (211,., Qum intimated that the scheduling of ether under the Poisons Act had had a very salutary effect in Ireland. Tire EDUCATION BILL.—Mr. W. H. &um, answering Sir William Harcourt, said the first reading of the Educa- tion Bill would be taken on Monday next, and the Mani- Pur debate might be taken on the day following the con- clusion of the report stage of the Irish Land Purchase Bill. The Government would continue to make every effort to bring about the prorogation by the end of July, and would shortly ask for the whole time of the House for its business. Tim NEWFOUNDLAND DIFFICULTY.—Sir JAMES FERGUS- SON, replying to a question said that if the telegram re- ceived from the Governor of Newfoundland correctly re- Ported the threat of a French officer, it amounted- to an Unwarrantable assumption of jurisdiction and inter- ference withthe rights of the British Crown. The atten- tion of the French Government had been called to the Matter. DISEASED ANIMALS. —Mr. JOHN LENG pressed Mr. Chap- lin to admit that the sending of the lungs of a suspected _animal from Livepool to London was needless, ' but Mr. talents said that considering the vast interests involved they should have the best possible advice, and after all the delay was short. THE BEHRING SEA BILL.—Mr. W. H. Slurs moved the second reading of the Bill enabling the Quern, by order of Council, to establish a close time for seals in the Behring Bea, so far as British subjects are concerned.—Sir lIARCOURT described the measure as wise and prudent.— ?Ir. J. CHAMBERLAIN, in supporting the Bill, and suggest- Lug safeguards, joined heartily with the First Lord of the 4-reasury in the feeling tribute to the worth of Sir John Macdonald, whose death, he said, would be an Inter- tational loss.—Sir GEORGE BADEN-POWELL having spoken. Pie Bill was read a second time. „THE LAND BlLL.—Afterwards the new clauses in the -Lush Land Purchase Bill, on the report stage, made fair Progress, and the House adjourned at 121.0. HOUSE OF LORDS.—TUESDAY. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the wooisack at ualf-past five o'clock. Several private and provisional order bills were forwarded a stage, and their lordships lose at twenty-five minutes to six o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—Tuzscay. The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. The morning sittings have been abandoned as the Land Purchase Bill has, by order of the house, precedence of all Private members' motions. QUESTIONS.—Mr. STUART WORTLEY gave Mr.D.Thomas an undertaking that in future, if possible, the district 11.0rts of mine inspectors should be published not later than May in each year. Mr. STANHOPE, replying to Mr. David Thomas as to the inconveßience caused by the de- lay in issuing ammunition to the'3rd Volunteer Battalion of the Welsh Regiment, said orders had been given for an immediate issue. Sir MICHAEL HICKS BEACH informed Mr. Penwick that as the Inflammable Liquids Bill had been withdrawn, he could not provide for the examina- tion in futute of petroleum vessels. Russia/4 JEWS. —Mr. W. H. SMITH, in reply to Mr. Jennings as to the threatened influx of 60,000 Russian Jews, said the consuls in the ports indicated had been asked to report by telegraph, and it would be undesir- abole to make any statement as to the views of the G yeErnment until they had some facts to go upon. toMore LAND BILL.—The House resumed consideration of anugorrt of amendments on the Land Purchase Bill,and Sexton, gy.r9int Samuel S proposed clauses were dealt with. Mr. ?uth in supporting a clause proposed by Mr. from what h g tenanc been in purchase to tenants whose y had been determined by process of law, said that e saw in Ireland a couple of years ago, he felt quite satisfied that if some means were not devised tor restoring the evicted tenants to their holdings it lsyould be next to impossible to maintain social peace in %hat country. Mr. Next on's amendrnent was rejected by a majority of 38. Mr. Ktiox proposed a clause enlarg- Ing the jurisdiction of the Land Commission under the liand Purchase Act of 1875, and conferring upon them certain powers of the Landed Estates Court and the land judges. The ATTORNEY-GENER.AL for Ireland opposed the clause, which was under discussion when the debate was adjourned at twelve o'clock. Bats WITHDRAWN. The Fire Inquest Bill was with- urawn. The Hares and Rabbits Bill was withdrawn. The House adjourned at ten minutes past twelve o'clock.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.—WEDNESDAY. The Speaker took the chair at 12.15, but it was not until 12.30 that a House was made. Trut Scown BILLS.—The House went into Committee 2_ll the Roads and Streets in Police Burghs (Scotland) Bill. which passed through Committee and was reported ITthe House. The Local Authorities (Scotland) Loans ills also passed through Committee. r, RATING OF MACHINERY (N 0.2 BILL.—The House of Inmons went. into Committee yesterday on the Rating 14 Machinery (No. 2) Bill, and Mr. Leighton immediate- moved to report progress, on the ground that there ; ad been no second-reading debate. Mr. WINTERBOTHAM, oPposing the moticn, said the Bill was founded on ‘ue report of a Committee of 1887, and it was carried through the second-reading stage last Year by 239 to 87. Sir HENRY JAMES sug- Fe•lted that instead of taking his present course Mr. !- p Ighton should assist the Committee in amending the Dill according to his own views. Sir William Houlds- !forth said the measure was urgently required by Lhe assessment committees. Mr. Joicey, in sup- Porting the motion to report progress, asserted that one of the members for Manchester, who had charge of a bill which stood before the present measure 911 the 7th April—the day of second reading,—was induced to withdraw his bill simply because there were no opponents to the Machinery Bill in the House at nine o'clock. He (Mr. Joicey) came down to the House at ten minutes past nine, and was met by rnore than one hon. member who in great glee told him bow cleverly the opposition to the bill had been "done." Mr. OseoaNr. MORGAN said the object of this motion was to throw out the bill by the side wind. The motion was defeated by 163 to 27, and the Committee proceeded :to deal with the CiatlSE S. progress being reported at 5.30. The Sale of Intoxicating Liquors on Sunday Bill was withdrawn, and the House adjourned at 5 45.

div.head: 'HOUSE OF LORICS.-MURSDAY,
div.p: 'HOUSE OF LORICS.-MURSDAY,
The Lord Chancellor took his seat at a quarter-past four. _ .
- The Earl of Shaftesbury took the oath and his seat..
Several private bills v'mre advanced a stage, and the House adjourned at tw'entr-five minutes to five. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—THIIRSDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. FREE EDUCATION.—It was resolved, on the motion of lir. JACKSON, that on Monday next tha House should re- solve itself into Committee to consider the making of further provision out of moneys to be provided by Parlia- Tnent for assisting education fn public elementary schools ln England and Wales. QuEsTioNs.—Sir J. GORST, in reply to Mr. S. MORE LYNCHING IN NEW ORLEANS.
Another Lynching case is reported from New Orleans. A negro tramp shot a farmer dead, but was only con- victed of theft. When liberated from gaol a few day ago he was seized and burned to death.

div.head: MR. PARNELL AND MRS. O'SHEA.
div.p: MR. PARNELL AND MRS. O'SHEA.

A London correspondent writes :—All the reports con- cerning Mr. Parnell's intended marriage with Mrs. O'Shea are, 1 am told on the best authority, devoid of founda- tion. The statements so far circulated are, upon the face of them, ridiculous fabrications.

div.head: TWO MEN KILLED AT BARNSLEY.
div.p: TWO MEN KILLED AT BARNSLEY.

Two men named Holdsworth and Bateman were killed in an accident which occurred on Wednesday night at a new colliery at Hoyle Mill, near Barnsley. They were engkged in walling the sides of the shaft, when the scaffolding collapsing' they were precipitated to the bottom, a distance of 40 yards. Two other men were injured.
THE CIIA.RGE AGAINST AIR. PARNELL.

The " National Press" on Tuesday renewed its attack upon Mr. Parnell, whom it accuses in plain terms of mis- applying certain funds, and it announces in unmistak- able language its intention to reiterate the charge in order to compel Mr. Parnell to take legal proceedings against the newspaper." The "National Press" also says that its secretary waited at its office on Tueiday, and will wait again to-day, to receive service of a writ from Mr. Parnell. The "Freeman's Journal" refers to the same subject. and calls upon the directors of the "National Press "to disavow the scurrilous article, in order that the writer may be discovered and exposed.

div.head: DESPERATE TRAIN ROBBERY BY BRIGANDS.
div.p: DESPERATE TRAIN ROBBERY BY BRIGANDS.

A Constantinople telegram of Monday describes the robbing of the Orient express by brigands on the previous night. The affair occurred near a small town between Constantinople an d Adrianople, the brigands tearing up the rails and hiding close by. The engine immediately on touching the disrailed portion of the ii ne was thrown over on its side,and the brigands, emerging, brandished their guns and despoiled the terrcr-stricken passengers, also ransacking the baggage. They finished up by carrying off four first-class passengers, for whose ransom they demanded Lq,ooo.

div.head: CROSSLEY .STREET MISSION AND CLUB
div.p: CROSSLEY .STREET MISSION AND CLUB
unom.
FOUNDATION STONE LAID BY LADY WALKER.

On Tuesday afternoon, the foundation stone of the new Crossley-street Mission and Club -Rooms was laid by the lion. Lady Walker. There was a profuse display of bunting on the scene of the cere- mony, and flags were also suspended from a number of windows some distance up Crossley-street. Among those present, in addition to Sir. A. B. and Lady Walker were the following :—The Rev. F. W. Willis, rector of Warrington. Mrs. Willis, Miss Willis the Revs. C. E. Jackson, D. S. Hodgson, T. W. Cook, and F. C. Timins (clergy of the Parish Church), Major Linton, Mrs. Beamont, Captain and Miss Willis, the Rev. J. Phillips and Mrs. Phillips, the Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs. Carleton, the Rev. F. and Mrs Slater, the Rev. T. E. Winder, the Mayor (Alderman Francomb), Mr. Ti. Davies, Mr. and Mrs. Vera Davies, Miss Pierpoint, the Misses Buckton, Alderman and Mrs. Wright, Messrs. N. B. Percival, and A. Woods, (churchwardens), Mrs. Stevenson, Mrs. Johnson Ferguson (Newton), Mr. John Dewhurst, Mr. S. Davies and others. Prayers were read by the Rector after which a hymn was sung by members of the Parish Church choir,Mr. J. Dewhurst presiding at the harmonium. The Rev. C. E. Jackson then delivered a very lengthy address. Many years ago, be said, there was established in the loft of an old building close by what we called a mission. Even regarded as the most temporary of all temporary arrangements it must both, as to its equipment and the character of its sur- roundings be regarded as the most unsavoury: and the most undesirable place that could well be imagined. It was a discredit to the wealthy and powerful church to which all present belonged. Regarded from the stand- point of their brotherhood, it reminded him of a tale that had come to them from the East, which represented a child asking for relief from a very influential member of his church. The tale told them that the child received from the powerful man's hand a crust of bread of very doubtful quality, and still more doubtful antecedents. Being very much surprised by a word which fell from the great man's lips, he said to him, "Is God really our Father; and are we really brothers ?" The important man replied ' Yes," and the boy instantly replied, "Then how dare you give to your poor brother such a mouldy crust as this which you have given to me ?" That was what he (the speaker) said with regard to the old mission room, which they hoped to leave at no distant date. The dawn of better things burst upon them two and a half years ago, when some cnildren, whose names it was only right he should mention—the children of Mrs. Gill and Mrs. Wright—originated a little sale of their own work, which they held in a private house, and with the proceeds of that sale they opened an account in the Old Bank at Warrington in the name ot Crossley-st. Building Fund. He would remind the audience that that account was still open, and yawning very wide to re- ceive their kind donations. Though they had been disappointed, they had made considerable progress. The subscription list now amounted to £903 12s. 10d., though there was still a deficit of £6OO. Thanking Lady Walker for her presence, the rev, gentleman said the sympathy shown by her that day was only an indication of the sympathy which was increasing between class and class in this country. He did not mean in charity or dis- tribution of alms, but a real growing of a feeling of de- termin ition on the part of the richer members of the community to endow those vast, gloomy, areas in which the poor lived, with some of those possessions which added so largely to the brightness and sweetness of their own. Lady Walker, who was a personal friend of the Queen, would be able to tell those present that that feel- ing of sympathy began with the Queen,and that she was interested and infcrmed about every movement which had for its object the amelioration of the condition of even the very lowest of her subjects. Mr. Jackson concluded by inviting Lady Walker to lay the foundation stone. Her ladyship then laid the stone, pronouncing as she did so, the formula : I declare this stone to be well and duly laid in the name I of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost." —Miss Willis, daughter of the rector, then presented to Lady Walker a beautiful bouquet: and the proceedings were concluded devotionally. A collection was made prior to the close which realised £24 is. 4d. Many ef the company present subsequently partook, by invitation,of refreshMents.in the mission room close by. The new building will be at the corner of Honwnod-st., and Brick-st, the piece of ground on which it will stand having been kindly presented by Sir Gilbert Greenall. There will be a mission room on the ground floor with seating for about 275 persons, and the room will be used for lectures, entertainments, &c., as well as for religious purposes. There will be club rooms for men, entered from Plopwood-st., there will also he on the ground floor a recreation room for youths, which will be provided with the usual appliances for games, and there will also be a large room which will be used for educational pur- poses, for young women and girls. The building is to be erected by Messrs. Gibson and Sons, and the total cost of the undertaking is estimated at about £1,500, some £3OO mere than was at first supposed. The building will pro- bably be completed in about three months.
