A CONTRACTOR'S REQUEST. Messrs. W. B. Jones and Co.. stationers, of Liverpool, sent a letter with reference to the printing of the medical officer's annual report. This tender was a Bs., and the work had cost £9, and Messrs. Jones wished the authority to pay them £lo.—The Clerk said the other tenders were LIO and upwards.—Mr. lirandreth objected to paying more than was tendered for. It was not fair to the other contractors.—The Clerk: We had a tender of £lO from a local firm.—The meeting authorised the payment of £8 Bs. only. ACCOUNTS.
Mr. Brandreth moved the passing of accounts amount- ing to £lB 18s. KECKIVICK BROOK.

Mr. Aaron asked if anything had been heard from the Local Government Board with respect to the pollution of Keckwick Brook.—The Clerk replied in the negative. —Mr. Aaron moved that the Clerk write to the Local Government Board and press for an answer in regard to the application in this matter.—The motion was seconded and carried.

div.head: ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES.
div.p: ST. AMBROSE CHURCH, WIDNES.

The corner stones of the new vicarage of St. Ambrose parish were laid, on Thursday afternoon, in a drenching shower of rain. The vicarage. which is estimated to cost £1,574, fronts rAlbert-road, and is to be built by Mr. 'Mime. of Seaforth, from plans by Messrs. Pierpoint and Fraser, architects, War- rington and Widnes. Of the six corner stones only three were to be laid, viz., by Mr. T. Sutton Timmis, J.P., Mr. E. Carey, and one by the churchwardens (Major Waring and Mr. H. Johnson). The others are to be laid on behalf of Mr. F. 11. Gossage, J.P., Mr. J. Brock, J.P., and Mr. G. Pilkington, J.P.—Dr. Preston, vicar of Holy Trinity, Runcorn, conducted the proceedings.—M r.Joh nson,vicar's warden,gare a financial statement which showed that £1,333 3s 2d had been raised towards the cost of the building. The chief donors were Mr. Timmis £3OO, Mr. Gossage .£125, and Mr. Brock £loo.—Mr. Carey in a brief speech, hoped the house would be the home of the vicars of St. Ambrose for many generations and he trusted it would last as long as the church, and that Mr. and Mrs. Le Bert would have long life and happiness in it.—Major Waring also spoke and addresses were delivered by the Rev. R. C. Hodg- kins (vicar of St. Cyprian's, Liverpool), Rev. G. H. Garrett (Widnes), and Rev. G. A. Le Bert (vicar of St. Ambrose). The stones having been laid, beauti- ful silver trowels, with ivory handles were pre- sented to Messrs. Timmins, Carey, Johnson, and Major Wareing.

div.head: ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN.
div.p: ASSAULTS ON THE POLICE AT RUNCORN.

John McDermott, of Heath-rd., and 'John Barnes of Weston, were brought before the Runcorn Matg- istrates, on Monday, to answer a charge of having been drunk and disorderly and refused to quit the Union Vaults. They were further charged with as- saulting P.C. Hughes. On Saturday tha men went into the vaults and were supplied with soda water. They were "not drunk nor sober" but they com- menced to use most disgusting language. Mrs. Sankey, the landlady, requested them to leave, but they refused, and she called P.C. Hughes to her aid. Immediately the officer entered the doorway Barnes gave him a violent blow under the ear, and both prisoners set upon him. lathe struggle the officer was severely mauled, and received a blow in the stomach, which partly disabled him. The prisoners got away. The Constable went home, washed the blood from his face,put on a suit of civilian's clothes, and went in search of his assailants,accompanisd by P.C. Edwards. He discovered McDermott, who threw off his coat, and,saying he would have another go, struck Hughes on the nose. The latter IStruk,-k back in self-defence, and eventually overcame his assailant and lodged him in the police cells. Barnes was afterwards apprehended at home.—Each pri- soner was fined in a total of 30s. or in default 21 days' hard labour.—Michael Connor, an ex-soldier, was charged with being drunk and disorderly and assaulting P.C. Pettinger. The prisoner when appre- hended behaved in a very violent fashion, and kicked and struck the officer. lie was fined 2s. 6d. and costs in each case.—John David Hughes, a young man, was charged with assaulting P.C. Worth. While the officers were struggling on the ground with the previous prisoner, Hughes kicked Worth severely. He was fined 105. and costs or 14 days' hard labour.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meting was held, at the Town Hall, on Tuesday night. The Rev. Dr. Gastaldi presided, and there were present Dr. McDougall, Messrs. S. Taylor, A. Salkeld, J. J. Hewitt, and G. Moss (clerk).

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE.

The School Attendance Committee reported that 116 persons had been summoned before them for contravention of the Education Act. 84 had ap- peared, and legal proceedings had been taken against 30 parents. The Visitors' reports showed a considerable falling off in the attendance, as com- pared with the corresponding month last year—from 83-3 to 764. The decrease was attributed entirely to sickness.—Mr. Taylor moved, and Mr. Salkeld seconded, the adoption of the minutes.—Dr. Mc- Dougall alluded to the large numbers of parents brought before the Committee, and asked for an ex- planation. He had been put upon the Committee against his will in order that his mouth might be closed in some mysterious way. He also wished to know why proceedings with regard to a breach of discipline at Greenway-road Board School had not been recommended on the minutes.—The Clerk said he did not consider it a matter which required re- cording. There was no recommendation, and the incident ended when it was dealt with by the Corn- mittee.—Mr. Howitt, replying to Dr. McDougall, mid no member liked to be on the School Atten- dance Committee. He had attended regularly as a duty, and he hoped the doctor would do so, and work harmoniously for the best interests of the children.—The minutes were passed.

div.head: EVENING CLASSES A- GREAT SUCCESS.
div.p: THE EVENING CLASSES A- GREAT SUCCESS.

The School Management Committee recommended that the Clerk be authorised to advertise for a head mistress for the Mill Brow Infant School. Her Majesty's Inspector reported with respect to the evening school :—" The school has made a good beginning, and is conducted with vigour and intel- ligence." The average attendance of the session was N. The grant amounted to £33 3s. The Clerk reported that the gross expenditure of the school was £6l Os. 6d., which was entirely covered by the receipts from school fees,.£2B Bs. 4d., and the grant. —The Inspector's report and the financial state- ment were considered highly satisfactory and encouraging for the future.—The minutes were passed and on the motion of Dr. McDougall the question of Berry's charges was referred to the Com- mittee.—The Clerk was instructed to write to Mr. Cook and Mr. Knowles and tell them not to pay any demand without the authority of the Board.
RUNCORN BOA.RD OF COMMISSIONERS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall on Thursday. Mr. S. Taylor presided and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman C.C., H. J. Grice, W. Mellor. H. White, J. Dobson, R. Abel, W. Hankin- son, E. lmison, E. W. Humphreys, and F. A. Lake (law clerk), and F. McDougall (medical officer of health.) The Chairman announced that Mr. E. Marshall the secretary was unable to attend to his duties through illness, and he proposed that Mr. J. D. Jones be the secretary pro tem.—Mr. Speakman seconded the motion which was carried.

THE INFLUENZA EPIDEMIC. The Medical Officer of Health reported that the Humber of deaths registered during the past month amounted to 70, of which 13 were due to epidemic influenza. The above 70 deaths showed an average death rate for the 12 months of 42 per 1,000 of the estimated population. A severe wave of epidemic influenza passed over the town during the last month, and the authority would observe with satisfaction that the death rate was a small one. There had been no cases of infectious disease re- ported for some time, and so far as he was aware the town was absolutely free from infectious disease at the present time. Influenza does not come within the Notifi- cation Diseases Act.—Mr. Dobson asked what was the present condition of the town with regard to the in fluenza epidemic.--Dr. McDougall replied that the wave was passing over very nicely,and was not nearly so severe as it was during the month of May. Ho could not re- member anything like this epidemic for the past 22 years, and he was glad to be able to say that he thought the wave of influenza was passing nicely.
WORK IN COMMITTEES.
The minutes of tue various Committees were passed

without discussions. It was resolved, on the recom- mendation of the Highway and Buildings Committee. that the following plans be approved :—Mr. Thomas Leach. jun., for the erection of a house in Heath-road. Mr. Wm. Nickson fer the erection of nine cottages in Stanley-street and Fisher-street. Warrington Land and Property Co. for the erection of six cottages in Porter - street, subject to the partitions dividing the yards being brick walls instead of wooden palings. Messrs. W. Farrell and Son, for the erection of seven shops at the corner of High-street and Savage's Bridge, adjoin- ing the Cocoa Rooms (two of them are lock-up shops with offices over), subject to there being no cellar openings or grids in the footway.—The Health Committee recom- mended that notices be served on the following persons to abate nuisances arising from overcrowding, and in the eventof non-compliance, tbat legal proceedings be taken: —Joseph Smith, 23, Mason-street, Thomas Johnson, 27. Masorestreet, Samuel Wilson, 39, Mason-street, William Large, 51, Mason-street, Mary Ann Smith, 55, Mason-st. That notices be served on theowner and occupiers of Nos 16 and 18, Bridge-street, to abate a nuisance and that in the event of non-compliance legal proceedings be taken The Finance Committee reported it was decided to give the trustees of the Loyal William Vltli Lodge of Odd- fellows six months notice to discharge the loan of £BOO.

THE NUISANCE INSPECTOR. On the motion of Mr. P. Speakman seconded by Mr. Dobson it was resolved that Mr. James Percival be appointed Inspector of Nuisances for the District for a further term of one year, at a salary after the rate of £125 a year.

div.head: NEW CHEMICAL LABORATORIES AT WIDNES.
div.p: THE NEW CHEMICAL LABORATORIES AT WIDNES.

The erection of the new laboratories for the United Alkali Co. has already been commenced, the site being the plot eeland between the Baths and Messrs. Gaskell, Deacon, and Co.'s luncheon room. _There are to be two distinct buildings which will be built of red brick, with terracotta dressings and the elevation will be made to harmonise with the dressings, THE CARTERS AND LURRYMEN OF WIDNES.

A meeting of carters and lurrymen was held in-Hutch- isson-street Cocoa Rooms, on Thursday night, when Mr. J. Kirkham of Bolton, president of the Amalgamated Carters and Lurrymen's Union delivered an address. It was decided to form a Widnes branch of the Union, and use every lawful means to reduce the working hours and improve the presint rate of wages.
THE CHARGE AGAINST A RUNCORN RELIEVING OFFICER.

I month ago Mr. Lea, one of the Guardians for Run- corn, brought a charge against Mr. Geo. Ward, the re- lieving officer, that he had forcibly ejected a woman named Mrs. O'Malley from his office. At the meeting of the Board, on Tuesday, Mr. Lea said he found that he had been rather mislead in the affair. The occur- rence had taken place a month before he was elected, and if the Guardians thought it best he should with- draw the charge.—At a late period of the meeting Mr. Ward was questioned on the subject, and denies that he had ever put Mrs. O'Malley or any other woman out of his office.—The subject was not farther investigated.

THEFT OF A MELODEON AT RUNCORN. At Runcorn Police Court,on Saturday, Thos.Saunders, of Church-st., and Samuel Cox, of Widnes-row, were charged with stealing a melodeon worth Bs.,the property of George Duckett, of Church-st. On Friday night P.C. Woodrow saw Cox with something bulky under his coat, and following him through several streets, searched him and found the melodeon. On reaching the Police Sta- tion, where the constable brought him, Cox stated that Saunders stole the article a week or two previously, while he kept "nix," and gave it to him to get 2s. upon it. The prisoners pleaded guilty, and were each fined £l, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. Saunders in- formed the magistrates that he only took the instrument for a lark.
DEATH OF MR. NEWBY CONWAY, FORMERLY OF RUNCORN.

We regret to have to record the death of Mr. Newby Conway, of Holly Bank, Frodsham, which occurred at his residence, on Thursday morning. For many years Mr. Conway was the sub-agent for the Bridgewater Trustees at Runcorn, and afterwards occupied the re- sponsible position of agent as Macclesfield. About 17 years ago he retired into private life and resided at South- port until about five years ago when he came to Frod- sham. While in Runcorn Mr. Conway was superintend- ent of Camden Wesleyan Sunday School. A gentleman of a genial and kindly disposition, he was highly res- pected by all who had the pleasure of us acquaintance. He had attained the age of 69 years. The interment will take place at Runcorn Cemetery. on Monday at three o'clock and the funeral arrangements are in charge of Mr. R. Morris, of High-st. SUMMER FesilioNs now Showing at J. & W. BUTTON'S Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt.
TRIPS TO NORTH WALES.

It will be seen from our advertising columns that the Liverpool and North Wales Steamship Com- pany, Limited, have made some slight alterations in their sailings ft,r the present month, and that pas- sengers by the St. Tuduo leaving Liverpool at 10.45 a.m. will have four hours on shore at Llandudno, also passengers leaving Liverpool by the Bonnie Princess at 1.35 p.m. can arrive at Llandudno in time to return by the St. Tudno, which is timed to leave that place at 4.45 p.m., and arrives back in Liverpool at 6.45 p.m. PaEmma SAFETIES, Cash or Hire.—GARLAND, Warrington. —Ade. ASSAULTING A CHESHIRE GIRL.

At the Wolverhampton Police Court, on Monday, Alfred Jones, a discl,arged soldier, of Peckham, London, was charged with indecently assaulting Ellen Johnson, a domestic servant, aged eighteen. The evidence showed that the prosecutrix was travelling from Ellesmere Port to her home at Kid- derminster, and when left alone in the carriage she was assaulted by the prisoner in a brutal manner. She endeavoured to jump from the carriage, but a passenger in a neighbouring carriage who had heard her screams walked along the footboard in time to prevent her. The train was going full speed at the time. The prisoner was charged when Wolverhampton was reached. He was remanded. SUMMER FASHIONS now Showing at J. ‘t. W. DUTTON'S Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. A WARNING TO GAS FITTERS.

_ At the St. Ilelens Town hail, on Monday, John Pilkington, a plumber of Brownlow-street, was charged with so connecting pipes to a gas meter as to prevent the meter from registering the quantii y of gas supplied, The Town Clerk (Mr. W. J. Jeeves) prosecuted on behalf of the Corporation. After stating that the defendant had rendered himself liable to a fine of £5, he explained that Mr. John Collins, of Hardsham -street, wanted to have some additional lights put in his cellar. Pilkington was employed to do the work, and he made the connec-. tiOia between the inlet pipe of the meter and the pipe by which the cellar was supplied from the meter. The meter was outside the connection, so that the gas for the:cellar lights did not pass through the meter, and in that way the Corporation accounts were materially affected. It might have gone on for years if it had not happened that a new meter was required. They did not allege any fraud against the defendant, but it was a piece of gross negligence on his part, and the Corporation wished to impress upon the plumbers of the town that they must use the greatest care in the work of connecting pipes to the gas meters.—Joseph Shakespeare, a gastitter in the employ of the Corporation, gave formal evi- dence, and the defendant, who pleaded guilty, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs. EMIGRATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the " Examiner" Office, by Cunard, anion, American. and other lines.— John Walker, agent, "Examiner' Office, Bewsey-at., Warrington,—Advt.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOL EVENING
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD SCHOOL EVENING
CLASSES.

An interesting gathering took place at Greenway- road Board School on Wednesday evening, when the successful students of the evening classes were presented with prizes and certificates by Mr. 11. c Dougall. There was a good attendance. In open- ing the proceedings Dr. McDougall said he was deputed by Air. James Pritchard, the worthy and respected chairman of the School Board, to express his deep regret that he was unable to be present that evening to present the prizes.—Mr. G. Moss, clerk to the Board, read the report of the Inspector on the classes, and said the number of passes was as follows :—Reading, 57; writing, 54 • arithmetic, 4.5; Fnglish grammar, 27. In the mathematics class which consisted of about 20 pupils, 19 passed in algebra, 2in mensuration, and in the shorthand class 9 were presented and 9 passed. He thought this was a highly satisfactory record. ('lear, hear.) —Mr. Moulton explained the principles on which the prizes were awarded, and then Dr. McDougall presented them to the students as follows : First Class Prize for passing in 5 subjects :—George Hunt, John Bowles, Wm. Wainwright, Thos. Broadhurst Walter, Caygill, E. Douglas, Wm. Edward Hough, Jno. W. Johnson, Dennis Chringhall, Harold Davies, Edward Henry Jones, Saml. Littler, E. W. Rowlands.—Second Class Prize for passing in 4 subjects :—E. Ward, Wm. Bunkhall, David Coventry, Arthur Dyer, John Corker, Hedley Powell, George E. Moss, John Kennan, Jas.Joncs, Arthur Moulton, Henry Holt, Thomas Hill, Wm. Ellison, S. Dutton, Thos. Carruthers, John A. Bate, Thos. Sweet- man, W. Thos. Howard, Charles Littler, James Henry Houghton. The following received illuminated certifi- cates of merit for passing in 3 subjects :—James Corker, Alf. E. Hind, Alf. Booth, Charles Hunt, John McLeod, Matthias Moors, John Coleman, W. Leach, Geo. Moores, Walter Yates, Robert Marsh, Thus. Henry Millington, mo. McCulloch, Arthur Sefton, Frank Sefton, Frank Thomas, Charles Hall, hobert Wright, Frank Rowlands. Two prizes given by the teachers for the highest number of attendances were won by Dennis Chringhall and Chas. Hall.

Dr. McDougall in the course of a speech to the students , congratulated them on the eminently successful way in which they had acquitted themselves at the examinations. He urged them to take advantage of all opportunities for self-improvement and for raising themselves in the social scale. Within the past few months there had been be- fore the public of Runcorn the question of a technical school. He did not know to what extent this school would be successful,but he hoped it might be successful. (Applause.)—Mr. Moulton proposed a vote of thanks to Dr. McDougall for distributing the prizes.—Mr. Moss seconded the motion,which was carried by acclamation. —Dr. McDougall having suitably responded, the proceed- ing terminated.

div.head: ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRINGTON FOOTBALL CLUB.
div.p: ANNUAL MEETING OF THE WARRING- TON FOOTBALL CLUB.

The annual racQting of the warrmgton Football Club was held in the Workmen's Club, Market Place, on Thursday evening, Mr. W. Tinsley, the president, in the chair, be being supported on the platform by Mr. J. E. Warren, hon. secretary, Mr. T. Pemberton, hon. treasurer, Mr. Councillor Pier- point, Mr. Adamson, and Mr. John Evans. There was a large attendance.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. JOLLEY.
div.p: THE DEATH OF MR. JOLLEY.

The CHAIRMAN said the first words he had to say were in regard to something which had occurred to that club, which they all deplored, the death of Mr. T. Jolley. It was with very great regret that they heard of their loss; and they were bound to feel it because he was evidently a promising player, and he (the chairman) would ask the permission of the meeting to send a message of condolence to the deceased's father and mother—he had no wife. A wreath had already been sent on behalf of the club. The proposal of the chairman was acquiesced

div.head: REPORTS.
div.p: THE REPORTS.

The Secretary's and Treasurer's reports were taken as read. The report of the lion. Sec. Mr. J. E. Warren contained the following :-- " Nothwithstandinc, the exceptionally severe winter we have again had 'a very husy and successful season. The first team have played 36 matches with the following result :-20 won, 9 lost. 7 drawn. Owing to the frost, four matches, Manchester Rangers, Broughton, Penarth, and Coventry, were nct played. For the same reason Pen-y-graig and Llanelly were arranged " draws" before the games commenced. The Lancaster and Oldham re- turn matches were postponed, but were decided later in the season. Another match was also played between Fair Turner's team (which included most of our first team players), and Valentine's team, at Swinton' for the bene- fit of a local charity, in return for which Mr. Valentine has engaged to bring a strong team to Warrington next season. The particulars of the dispute with the Llanelly club have already been made public. My committee consider we have been very badly treated in the matter, and the facts have been placed before the Welsh and English Unions, with a view to getting compensation from the Llanelly club for the loss of a gate. The report stated the " A" team had had one of the most successful seasons since the formation of the club, having lost but one fixture. The second team had won 12 out of 18 matches. _

The report of Mr. T. Pemberton, lion. treasurer,con- tained the following : " The balance sheet placed before you will compare favourably with previous balance sheets. We have had matches cancelled by frost, and have a match owing to us by the Llanelly F.C. We have spent a large sum of ' money on plant. Taking the receipts, the subscriptions ' are slightly less owing to the resignations of honorary members. The net gate last season was £763 ss. 81d., this season £771 12s. 90. The sports this season re- sulted m a profit of £52 us. Bd., after charging the accounts with a new number board, against a profit of £24 Bs. 3d. last season. There.has been an extraordinary expenditure on the ground. The railway fares have in- creased owing to the long journeys to the north of Eng- land and South Wales. The item for jerseys, bags,gic., is larger than the previous year owing to one of the teams having had new bags. flio other expenses are slightly better." Tho accounts allowed receipts amounting to £lO2O 17s. 141., including a balance from 1800 of £53 6s. Bd, and an expenditure of £965 19s. 81-d., leaving a sum of £54 in hand. The principal items of the expenses were as follows :—Capping fence, boarding stands, and sundry joiner's wcrk, £lO3 , 19s. 5d.; railway fares. £lB7 108. Bd.; dinners and refreshments to players, visiting teams, and com- mittee, £lO7 16s. 7d.; hotel expenses, .E9O 16,. 5d ; insurance of three teams, fee to Medical Association and amount paid to injured players (less claims from Insurance Society, £120), £47 Is. Bd.--Mr. Dixon said he considered the balance sheet a very fair one with one or two exceptions. As to the £lO3 198. sd. h spread e considered this would have been better over two or three years, as it was a large item for one year. He also thought that £2l 15s. w large item for a doctor's fees, embrocations knee caps, caps, &c., considering that the club had pa'i'd £47 is. Bd. to the Medical Association. He also objected to such large expenditure for hotel expenses, lie would prefer more money invested in stock in case of a bad season. He expressed his satisfaction at the profit on the sports £5O, and thought the balance sheet generally reflected great credit on the society and treasurer.—The Treasurer e beenagreed with Mr. Dixon that the £lO3 would better mter spread over several years, but said the item would not occur next year. The item of 1.!21 15s. for doe- tors fees, &c., was extraordinary, but resulted from having to send a man to Liverpool to see the specialist Mr. Owen Thomas. 3lr. Dixon thought there was something fishy somewhere.— Councillor Pierpoint thought Mr. Dixon was out of order for using this expression. Certain members had sustained injuries necessitating the best medical advice, but the Committee themselves were not quite satisfied, and a special Committee had been appointed to deal with the matter.--Mr. Dixon said he did not mean his expression to apply to the Committee at all.—Couticillor Pierpoint Then you withdraw it of course.—The n.ports were adopted.

div.head: ELECTION OF PRESIDENT.
div.p: ELECTION OF PRESIDENT.
I Councillor PIERPOINT proposed the re-election of Mr. Tinsley as president, Mr. EVANS seconded, and Mr. Tinsley was unanimously re-elected with acclamation, the Chairman thanking the meet— ing.

SPECIAL RESOLUTIONS. Rule 2 was altered to read "That the annual sub- scriptions become due on the Ist of September." The following motion was put and passed.—That Rule 4 be altered, to read 'That the Acting Officers shall consist of a President, Three Captains, Two Sub-Captains, Honorary Treasurer, and Honorary Secretary, who shall form part of the Com- mittee; such Committee with ths above excep- tions, shall consist of eight non-playing mem- bers, and also the two umpires by virtue of their office." Itwas resolved " That the annual subscrip- tion for ordinary members joining the Warrington F. C., after this date, remain 4s. with an entrance fee of 55." It was resolved that the annual sub- scription for playing members be reduced to 2s. 6d., with an entrance fee of 2s. 6d.
THE DEATH OF MR. JOLLEY.

. Councillor Pierpoint, who had now taken the chair, referred to the loss the club had sustained by the death of Mr. Jolley, and read letters from Mr. S. Crosfield, captain of the Warrington Cricket Club; Mr. Edward Roper, Mr. A. G. Steel, Mr. D. Q. Steel, and Mr. Hornby, captain of the Lancashire team expressing deep regret at the death of Mr. Jolley.

div.head: ELECTION OF OFFICERS AND COMMITTEE.
div.p: ELECTION OF OFFICERS AND COMMITTEE.

The following were elected :—Secretary. Mr. E. Warren; Treasurer, Mr. Thos. Pemberton; Audi- tors, Messrs. W. Bibby and T. Wallington; Reporter for fist team, Mr. Geo. Archer; Reporter for "A team, Mr. F. Howard; Captain of first team, Mr. H. Ashton ; sub-captain first team, Mr. J. W. Evans; captain "A " team, Mr. T. Davies; sub-captain "A" team, Mr. W. Antrobus ; captain second team, Mr. Warburton; sub-captain second team, Mr. T. Lally; umpire first team, Mr. W. Povey ; umpire "A" team, Mr. John Holmes; umpire second team, Mr. Boyle. Committee: Messrs. Hewitt, Adamson, Smith, Evans, Bowers, Thos. Barnes, jun., W. Dillon, and W. Pierpoint. Trustees: Messrs. G. Smith and J. Evans.
A CHILD DROWNED IN HOWLEY BROOK.

John Norton, aged three years, son of Patrick Norton, labourer, Lord Nelson-st., was drowned yesterday afternoon in the llowley Brook. The deceased had his dinner, and left home to play by the brook, which, in consequence of heavy rains, was full of water. He was standing on a stone floating corks, when he fell into the water, and was carried under a culvert. Another boy raised an alarm, and Thomas Hayes,who happened to be near, got into the brook and rescued the child, and con- veyed him home, where he was discovered to be dead. The Howley Brook has been the scene of the deaths of several children, and recommenda- tions have been made by coroner's juries that it should be stopped up. That work is now being slowly proceeded with by the Corporation, but it has not been far enough advanced, as our frequent record shows, to obviate the recurrence of fatal accidents.

div.head: DEATH OF A LOCAL CRICKETER.
div.p: DEATH OF A LOCAL CRICKETER.

General regret was expressed in Warrington on the announcement of the death of Mr. Thos. Jolley, a member of the Warrington Cricket Club. and son of Mr. G. Jolley, which took place at his home in Allen-street, at 10-30 on Tuesday morning. The deceased was seized with peritonitis,following upon an attack of influenza, about a fortnight ago, and although hopes were entertained, by his physician, Dr. Adams, of his recovery,during Vv.) latter portion of last week,a relapse occurred on Monday evening, resulting fatally on Tuesday morning. Only quite recently Mr. Jolley distinguished himself in the cricket match at Old Trafford on Whit-Monday between Lancashire and the next 17. His last appearance in the cricket field was on May 23rd, against Leyland. Deceased was in his 24th year Nnt nnly watl thc, cicc.caacti one of arrington's best exponents of the game of cricket, but he was alsoan excellent football player, having been connected. with the Warrington club for many years, and a prominent member of the "A" team. The deceased was employed as a wiredrawer at Whitecross works. It has been arranged that the funeral will take place to-morrow (Sunday) afternoon. It is under- stood that a large number of the members of the Football and Cricket Clubs, besides deceased's work- fellows, will attend to manifest theiriregret at his early death. The members of the "Lord Elliott" lodge of Druids, of which Mr. Jolley was a member,. will also follow the remains to the grave.

div.head: INFLUENZA IN WARRINGTON.
div.p: INFLUENZA IN WARRINGTON.
SAD FATALITIES.

On Saturday morning a woman, aged 28, named Ann Kettle, of 12, Bissell-st., wife of George Henry Kettle, engine driver in the employ of the London and North-Western Railway Co., died at her resi- dence of influenza combined with pneumonia and abortion. On Tuesday, her husband, aged 31, died from influenza combined with pneumonia. Mrs. Kettl3 was the first to be attacked, and Mr. Kettle was seized quite suddenly by the prevailing malady on Tuesday night week, he having previously been a strong, healthy man. Five children are left young orphans by these sad and untimely deaths. The deceased couple were attended by Dr. Adams, of Bewsey-st., who has at the present time about 150 cases of influenza in hand. Since the middle of April he has had under treatment between 400 and 500 cases of the disease, out of which 14 have proved fatal. It may fairly be assumed from his experience, there being some fifteen or sixteen medical practitioners in the town, that there are not fewer than 1,000 cases of influenza at present in Warrington. It is reasurring, however, to learn from Dr. Adams, that the epidemic is on the de- cline so far as our district is concerned. Dr. Adams estimates that there cannot be fewer that,. 100 men suffering who are employed at Dallam and, Bewsey forges. Dr. Brookes states that Messrs.. Monks, Hall, and Co., for whom he acts profes- sionally.have about 30 men off with the complaint. About 45 men employed at the Whitecross works are at present invalids through it, and one of the employes at that establishment died of it, yesterday morning. A baby also died the same morning in the town of the disease. Seven deaths are reported as having occurred in Warrington from the malady during last week.

GRAPPENHALL. Influenza is still at it height in the village of Grappen- hall and in many of the surrounding farms. One of the sufferers from it is Mr. James Burrows, formerly sexton of the Parish Church. Mr. Burrows is considered the oldest inhabitant of Grappenliall, being 85 years of age. He has for the last 40 years been employed by the Dares- bury Highway Board as roadmender for the Grappenhall district.
STRIKE OF JOINERS AT ST. HELENS.

The dispute in the building trade at St. Helens is still unsettled, and the whole of the 200 joiners and carpenters who came out on strike on Monday morning still remain out. At an interview be- tween the men's representatives and the masters at the Fleece Hotel, on Tuesday night, the masters offered to sign the amended rules of the society, on condition that any notice in regard to a change in wages or hours of I labour should terminate at any time during the year. The men, however, insisted that all notices should ex- pire on the Ist May, otherwise disputes between them and the masters would be frequent during the slack seasons. No arrangement was arrived at, and the strike continues without any hope of an early settlement. The plumbers are agitating for an increase in their wages. They claim an advance from 711td. to 81d.per hour, and i if the masters decline to grant t they will come out on strike. It is stated that the masters have offered to ,give Bd. ner hour, but this is not satisfactory to the men. On Thursday the plumbers, numbering about twenty, came out on strike. The dispute does not extend t,e. plumbers employed in the gas and water departments of the Corporation. At a private meeting of the St. Helens Trades Council on Wednesday night the brick- layers reported that the employers had acceded to the si:gning of the amended rules. The joiners and plumbers reported that they had not yet been able to arrange terms with their employers, and in accordance with the rules of the Council the Council decided to support the men in the struggle.

div.head: _BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: _BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
THEFT BY A WOMAN.

At the Warrington Poll& Court, on Wednesday, Mar- garet Tully, wife of John Tully, was charged with steal- ing from thehouse of Michael Tully, Cloth Hall-yard, on Monday last a pair of trousers, the properey lf Edward Tully, her brother-in-law. The parties both lived at the house of Michael Tully, the woman's father-in-law. She was sentenced to seven days' ipprisonment.

div.head: TRANSFER OF LICENSES.
div.p: TRANSFER OF LICENSES.

At the Warrington Police Court, on Monday, the 'following transfers of licenses were granted :—From Joseph Taylor of the Norton Arms Hotel, to John Samp- son; from John Darbyshire, of the Boar's Head, to Wm. Morton; from Wm. Walker, 16, and 18, Greenall-st., to Lillie Mary Nevin; from John Newns to Sarah Ann Robinson of Chorley-st. Temporary authority to sell until next transfer day was granted to James Legh, for the Red Lion Inn, in lieu of John Shepherd and to Mary Ann Lea, Watkin-st., in lieu of her father.
THEFTS BY A LODGER.

At the Borough PoHoc Court, on Tuesday, Patrick Oaffev was charged with stealing between 11 o'clock on Saturday night, and 8 o'clock on Sunday morning, Bs. 6d., the property of Bryan Noon, 35, Foundry-st., and 94d. an ounce of tobacco, and a pocket knife, the property of Patrick Welsh, a lodger at the house. It appeared that Mrs. Noon placed her purse in her dress pocket and turned the dress inside and tied the pocket, and the prisoner, who slept with Welsh, and came to lodge at the house on Saturday night, got up and stole Bs. 6d. from it and also the articles belonging t 3 Welsh.—The prisoner was fined .20s. and costs.

div.head: WIFE DESERTION.
div.p: WIFE DESERTION.

Thomas Maskell, was charged at the Borough Police -uourr, hie wife Mary Maskell. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant, anu the couple had been married four years. On the 10th of March they were living in Victoria-st., and the defend- ant's mother, his two sisters, and his brother took the whole of the furniture away. The defendant unscrewed the bed the baby was sleeping on, and told his wife he was going to live with another woman and he would take it for to sleep on it, and straw was good enough for ids wife to lie on. He had stabbed her with a knife and bad often stopped out all night, giving no explanation for his absence. He loft her after removing the furni- ture and never returned. He said he could never do anything right for his wife ; and she made such rows and she had left him once, An order was made for an allowance of 103. a week, the order to be put in force for a month, to allow him time to pay.

div.head: WOMAN-BEATING RUFFIAN.
div.p: A WOMAN-BEATING RUFFIAN.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Mon- day, Thomas Knockton, was brought up on a a warrant charged with assaulting Mary Knockton, his sister, on the 4th of May. A constable stated that on that date he saw the defendant in Winwick-st., with a crowd of people round him, and kickinc, and thumping the complainant. When the defendant saw him he ran away, but witness knew him and summoned him though he did not appear to the summons. The complainant corroborated the officer's evidence, and said she could not tell what the assault wag for.—Chief Constable Hunt said the woman had a fearful pair of black eyes when she came to complain of her brother's assault. Their father had some time ago come before the court and said he was in great fear of the defendant.—The Chairman (to the prisoner): Why don't you tackle some well built young fellow your own age? I suppose you would prefer to fight with an old man of 70 or a girl, so that you -would not have your own precious skin touched.—Alder- man Harrison: None but a coward would ever abuse a female as you abuse this girl.—The Chairman said there was a sheet of charges against the prisoner all for brutal attacks on people, one of them committed a little while -ago on Jane Jones.—The prisoner was sentenced to two month's imprisonment with hard labour.
A WOMAN SAVAGELY ASSAULTS AN OLD MAN.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday, Jane Johnson, a young married woman, who now made her 33rd appearance, was charged with assaulting James Johnson, her father-in-low, aged 70, at his house in Brown-st., off Winwick-st., also with wilfully damaging some pictures and crockery there, to the amount of 10s., on the same occasion. She had been some time in Man- chester, and returned on Saturday night, calling at the house about a quarter-past ten.—The Chief Constable said she did not live with her husband, because he could not live with her. She had been living about Manches- ter, but returned on Saturday night, and went to the prosecutor's house drunk, and asked for her husband. The prosecutor was alone in the house, and she took up a hammer and smashed four pictures and some crockery, value 10s. He did all he could to restrain her, and she turned round and said, "Now, you shall have it," and struck him three times on the head, with, as he sup- posed, a knife, so that he bled most profusely.—The pro- secutor, who appeared with his head bandaged, corrobo- rated this statement.—A piece of wood was produced with which the defendant admitted she had struck the old man, but said he struck her first, and she used no knife.—Mr. Hunt : The house was like a slaughter-house, there was so much blood.:—She was sent to gaol for two months' hard labour for the assault, and for an addi- tional month's hard labour for the damage.

div.head: STEAT ING THE GOODS OF A FURNITURE DEALER.
div.p: STEAT ING THE GOODS OF A FURNITURE DEALER.

John Norman was charged at the Warrington Police Court, with stealing between the 26th of March and April 6th, by converting to his own use, a quantity of goods value about £5, purchased from Messrs. A. and E. Cowen, house furnishers, Rylands-st. Mr. P. Davies appeared for the prosecution. He stated that the pri- soner entered into an agreement on the 13th of Decem- ber last for the hire of the goods, a flock bed, a table, three chairs, a timepiece, and a fender ; the total value .of which was £5 Bs. 6d., which he had to pay off at the rate of 2s. 6d. per week. The agreement was read over, and thoroughly explained to him, and it stipulated that the articles were not ta be removed without the written consent of the firm, and were to remain their property till all was paid for. The goods were however, removed, and the owner had considerable difficulty in finding what had become of 'hem. and the goods themselves could not be found. There had been a sum of 12s. 6d. paid on them :—Abraham Cowan, confirmed Mr. Davies's state- ment, and said the prisoner lived at No. 4 Oliver-st,. when the goods were supplied to him. Witness brought an action in the County Court, to recover the gooas from the prisoner.—Mr. Davies said that the Judge held that there was not sufficient identification of the goods, and the plaintiff lost his case.—The prisoner pleaded not guilty, stating that a woman he lived with had sold them while he was at St. Helens, to Mr. Gregg. . On being told that he was responsible for her doing so, he, with some _reluctance, pleaded guilty; and was sentenced to six weeks hard labour.
ROBBERY rnom A LOCH-lIP SRO?.

At the Borough Police Court, yesterday, Michael Garity -bircksetter's labourer, 4, Glass House-yard, and James Bibby, 37, Scotland-road, were charged with entering ..some time between 9 p.m. on the 3rd inst. and 9.30 a.m. on the 4tit inst., the lock-up shop of James Harper, 123, Sankey-st., and stealing therefrom three pairs of men's boots, one pair of pliers, one pair of nippers, one pair of pincers, one bass and one man's tweed jacket value in all £2—Chief Constable Hunt said the prosecutor in the morning at half-past eight missed the articles and found the back door wide open. The matter was reported to the police, and Detective-Sergeant Monaghan made inquiries 'and found that the prisoner's had been selling the articles at Mr. Leslie's and Mr. Gibbon's, and he subsequently „apprehended them, and Mrs. Leslie and Mrs. GibbNi,

identified Garity as having brought some of the articles for sale. Bibby told Monaghan that he alone was guilty; and in court he repeated this, stating that Garity had nothing to do with the matter. Garity pleaded not guilty. The Chief Constable said there was proof of the two men acting in concert after the robbery. They were remanded till to-day.
CHARGES AGAINST DRFAULTING APPRENTICES.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, Mr. Arthur Browne prosecuted on behalf of Messrs. John Platt and Sons, fustian cutters, the following apprentices for ab- septing themselves from the service of the firm :—Ellen Brannan. a child, was first charged. She and another apprentice of the firm, Ellen Lomax, had left their work and walked together to Manchester and back. She had put the firm to an expanse of 2s. An order was made for her return to work and pay the costs and Is. a week.— Mary Jane Clara had put the firm to £1 15s. expenses, and her father John Clare was summoned with her as surety for her carrying out her indentures. He had denied signing the indenture, and stated he could not. read or write, but admitted signing it on being shown his signature, then said the date was wrong. The girl had been working both at Mr. Wilkinson's and Mr. Bol- ton's since leaving. Mr. Wilkinson had discharged her on learning she was an absconded apprentice. An order was made for return to work and payment of £1 15s. by the girl at 2s. per week, and £1 by the father at the rate of 2s. per week, costs being added in each case. In the case of Mary Ellen Woodhead who had returned to work but since perforraed it very unsatisfactorily, an order was made for payment of the loss 3s. and costs.—Hannah Lomax was ordered to return co work and pay the loss 2s. and costs.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY.—Before Alderman Burgess (in the chair) and Councillor Voisey. DRUNKENNESS.— Elizabeth Lawrenson and Patrick Brannon, a soldier, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Buttermarket-st. on Friday evening. Brannon was also charged with assaulting Lawrenson. The charges were proved by P.C. He and another man were fighting, both having their shirts off, and their faces covered with blood. It appeared that the other man had been kicking his wife and the defendant interfered, hence the fight.— The case was dismissed, the Mayor remarking that he would not have summoned the defendant at all ; a man must be a coward who would stand and see a man kick his wife.

THE OCCASIONAL COURT. Before Mr. Ziba Armitage. DRUNKENNESS.—On Monday, Annie M'Cormick was charged with being drunk at Golborne on May 30th.—She was fined ss. or seven days' imprisonment. Ihe fine not being forthcoming she was sent to prison,—At the same court, on the same date,Ellen Bower was charged with a similar offence, and was fined ss. and costs, which was paid.
WARRINGTON COUNTY perry SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before Major Piektnere, Mr. Jolla White,
and Capiain Withington. DRUNK.—John Conway, drunk at Houghton Green on the 20th ult, was fined 24. 6d.

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Frederick Yardley, drunk and disorderly at Rixton, was fined 2s. 6d. and Costs. FURIOUS DRIVING.--Jonathan Broadhurst,for furiously driving a horse and spring cart in ,Woolston, on Whit Monday, was fined 10s. and costs. _

CIitIIISLTY TO A HORSE.—William Hewitt was charged by Inspector Doughty with cruelly ill-treating a horse by working it while in an unfit state, at Houghton, on the 12th ult. The inspector said the horss was exces- sively lame on the near, fore leg, and was drawing 30 cwt. of manure in a cart, which the defendant said was 14cwt. Mr. Taylor, veterinary surgeon,said the animal was suffering from contracted tendons, and totally unfit for work. The Bench proceeded to view the horse, and as the result, fined the defendant in the costs, and or- dered him to work the horse no more on the road. The defendant's father, Enoch Hewitt, the owner of the horse, was also summoned, but prevented by illness from appearing. BICYCLING ON THE FOOTPATII.—Henry Broadhead, for riding a bicycle on the footpath on the 14th ult.' on Liverpool-road, Great Sankey, was fined is. and costs. A ROWDY GANG INVADE LICENSED PREMISES.—Jona- than Broadhurst, Wm. Shaw, James Melia, Richard Warburton, Frank Harrison, Lathe or Forster, Sarah Foster, his wife' and James Rogers, all of whom were stated to be employed in Warrington, were charged with being disorderly and also with refusing to quit the Horse and Jockey Inn, Wonlston, on Whit Monday. Mr. A. Browne, instructed by the Licensed Victuallers' Association, appeared for the prosecution. He stated that the defendant Broadhurst was the man just con- victed for furiously driving, and he was doing so to es- cape the police who had been sent for by the landlord of the inn.—James Massey,thelandlord, deposed that about half-past six on Whit Monday night, he heard a disturb- ance in his yard and found the defendants there,and that Warburton had struck a horse on the nose in front of the inn. He asked why he had done this aid Warburton threatened to hit him. Witness told them to go or he wouki bring a constable. They remained a considerable time. Mrs. Forster charged witness with knocking her husband out of the cart, lie having, witness had heard, tumbled out through being drunk. Witness contradicted her and she " smashed " at him and struck him. She pushed him down and his son pushed her down. War- burton,Shaw,and Broadhurst rushed at him and thumped him. Three of the defendants including Shaw tackled a man named Bolton, and thumped him on the ground. Warbur- ton came up to tup vvitness,and he grabbed him and tore Ins necktie off. Witness had to bolt himself in doors and send for a policeman. Mrs. Forster then took her boot off and broke a window with it. Nicholas Massey, and Joseph Massey his son, corroborated, and said Broadhurst and Melia struck him about the eye.—John Bolton, Ship Canal labourer, said he went to the son's assistance and Warburton, Shawl and another got him down and gave lihn two black eyes. Mrs. Forster was the worst of the lot.—James Dumble corroborated.—The defendants all pleaded not guilty, most of them alleging prior assault on them as provocation. Broadhurst, Shaw, Melia, Warburton, and Sarah Forster were each fined 20s. and costs, and Harrison, James Forster and Rogers ss. and
costs each.

Mr. Burton appeared for the defendants —l-cilliam Murray was fined ss. and cbsts for being drunk and disorderly and a similar penalty was imposed upon James Almond, James Daives and John Thompson for a like offence.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

A.. Mold was 26 yeii:s-7,1-ge on Saturday, and thought he would do something to commemorate such an auspicuous event, so he took five Sussex wickets for 11 runs in) the first innings. He was a bit more merciful when Sussex went in a second time, and oily knocked down four for 22. However, nine wickets for 33 runs is not bad on a Man's birthday.

That lively individual, Jimmy Ross, has broken out in a fresh place. He is now one of the stars of the Preston C.C., and can wield the willow to some tune. Although he was almost a stranger to cricket some two years back, the old county player Cornelius Coward, has tutored Jimmy so well that he can now bat in first-class style. Ia the last three Instche3 for Preston he has scored 36, 18, and 14, and he is just about the smartest. fielder-in the team.

If "a rolling stone gathers no moss" what must a oriohoter be who has played for four counties, and is qualified for a fifth? Not much good, you would think; but Shilton, who has earned this distinction, is a very fair all round player, and might be a better if he did not think there was only one good cricketer in the country. He has in turn played for Northumberland, Durham, Yotkshire, and Warwickshire, and resides in Stafford- shire. He was born in Coventry.

div.head: FOOTBALL.
div.p: FOOTBALL.

The balance sheet of the Aston Villa F.C. has been issued, and after starting with a balance in hand of £261 6s. 40., they finish with one on the wrong side of £125 17s Bd., but they have paid players in advance for next season no less than £275 16s. Bd., and have owing to the Club £2O 6s. Bd.. whilst their pavilion, stands, Sm., are valued at £459 155., so that tho Villa are clear', out of debt. Their gate money reached £3,193 15s. 3d., and players' wages £1,836 12s. 2d.

The Salford Football Club have once more issued their annual balance sheet, and a glance at the detailed ex- penditure shows what a complicated and expensive in- stitution a football team can become. A trivial item of £93 for jerseys, hosiery, &c., with £29 for washing same, will show that expense is no object.

At the annual May meeting of the Oldham Football Club, held on Friday, it was stated that the result of the year's working was considered satisfactory. Notwith- standing that the club had on many occasions to place indifferent teams in the field, through calls made on their players by Lancashire County and Wales and other causes, yet out of the 33 matches played they had suc- ceeded in winning 17, whilst of the remainder six were drawn and 10 lost. Financially the club have made a profit of £315 on the season's working. In reply to questions it was announced that the team for next season would be practically the same as last, the only exception being Nolan, their crack half-back, who it is understood is seeking pastures new.

The sum spent by the Entertaining or Catering Depart ment will make some folks eyes open as wide as the edibles have made the orifices of those who enjoyed the good things, and £126 is a big item to swallow; but even this is eclipsed by the" towers," for the visit to London and the little trip at Easter have absorbed £258. A good feature of the management is observed in the steady in- crease of invested money, and after all is said and done, the club stands worth over £9OO, and have £5OO of this amount in Salford Corporation Stock. The accident Fund has been drawn on to the extent of £5O for allow- ances, and though there is a fully-qualified• "medicine man "appointed, the peculiar expenditure of £5 10s. for embrocation might warrant the inquiry as to whether it was for limbs or feelings.

div.head: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: ELECTION INTELLIGENCE.
MR. VICTOR. CAVENDISH ELECTED.
Mr. Victor Cavendish, Liberal Unionist, w-a—s—o'n Tues- day elected as member for West Derbyshire without opposition.
CITY OF LONDON.

The .Sheriff of London sat on Wednesday to receive nominations to fill the vacancy in the representation of the city caused by the death of Sir R. Fowler. Sir Reginald Hanson, Conservative, was the only candidate nominated, and there being no opposition he was declared duly elected.
PAISLEY ELECTION. ANOTHER LIBERAL VICTORY.

When the poll opened on Monday morning, many sup- porters of the respective candidates—Mr. M'Kerrell (Unionist) and Mr. Dunn (Gladstonian Liberal)—were waiting to record their votes. In the breakfast hour the polling was very brisk, and again there was a heavy poll at one o'clock, when several of the largest works closed for the day. A further heavy poll resulted between six and eight o'clock. Each party issued a large quantity of electioneering literature, and conveyances of all sorts were freely employed. The counting of the ballot papers was concluded about ten o'clock, the result being a Liberal victory, as follows : Mr. William Dunn (L) Mr. R.M.M'Kerrell (U)... 2,807

Liberal majority 1,338 The sweeping majority for the Liberal was a complete surprise. It was anticipated that the victory would be a Liberal one, but the extent of the majority was alto- gether unexpected, and the result was received with loud and prolonged clie2ring, by acrowd assembled out- side the Sheriff's buildings. In addressing his Committee after the declaration of the poll, Mr. Dunn said the re- sult would be a message of peace to Ireland, and a mes- sage of hope to the great leader of their party.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THE NEW BILL

The" Daily News" says :—Just before the Easter re- cess it was ordered that the Manchester Ship Canal Bill should be referred to the Committee of Selection. Mr. Ritchie intends to move the discharge of that order with a view of substituting another referring the bill to a. hybrid committee of seven members, four to be momin- atad by the house and three by the Committee of Selec- tion.
MANCHRSTER CORPORATION AND THE DIRECTORS.

At a meeting of the Manchester City Council held on Wednesday the promotion of thelomt Corporation Bill in regard to the loan to the Ship Canal Cbmpany was con- firmed. A strong opinion was expressed that the Coun- cil should be represented on the Board of Directors by not less than five members, an 1 the Mayor promised to see that this view was enforced. ACCIDENT AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday, a labourer named Thomas Morris, employed in the construction of the Bridgewater Locks, had three fingers ot his left hand cut off by a travelling crane. Morris was pulling himself' frorn the dam, and had his fingers on the metals of the tramway, when the crane came along, and injured him, as stated. Dr. McDougall dressed his wounds. A SELECT COMMITTEE APPOINTED.

In the House of Commons,on Thursday, on the motion of Mr. Ritchie it was resolved—'• That the order kl2th May) committing the Manchester Ship. Canal Bill to the Committee of Selection be read and discharged ; that the bill be referred to a select committee of seven members, four to be nominated by the House and three by the Committee of Selection;. that the petitions presented in pursuance of standing order 210 be referred to the Corn. mittee and dealt with pursuant to the said standing order, that three be a quorum."

div.head: BOY DROWNED, IN THE; CLAY PITS.
div.p: A BOY DROWNED, IN THE; CLAY PITS.
DEATH OF THE CHILDS FATHER,

An inquest was held by Mr. S. Brighouse, coroner, at the Bowling Gregn Inn, on Tuesday afternoon, concerning the death of Walter Ernest Humphreys,' on Sunday afternoon through his fall- ing into a clay pit in a 'biickfield off Wellfield-st. Elizabeth Ann Humphreys,.motherof the deceased, who was in great distress, said the child left his home 25,Percy-st., about half-past two, on Sunday after- noon, with his brother and little sisters, She never saw him again alive. His little sisterrage a; ran, home during the afternoon, and told her Walter was drowning. Wit- ness ran immediately to the pit, and found that he had been taken out of the pit. They said he was alive but she thought he was not. Dr. Braide came, and did all he could, but said he knew it was useless. The brickfield was an open space where all the children about played. —Police Inspector Bowen stated that Mrs. Humphreys's husband, a foreman of public works, had died that morning from consumption.—Frank Humphreys, aged 10, said he was in the brickfield with the deceased (his brother) and his sisters. They were about 100 yards from the pit. He did not see the deceased near it or hear him scream but saw Mr. Tildsley trying to get him out.—Joseph Tildsley, owner of the bnckfield, said he saw some children wasting sand and taking it away, and drove them away. They were trespassers there. He had £2O worth of damage a year done there by children, besides loss through thefts of timber and coal. He saw the deceased near the edge of the pit, but the child did not see him,and on. turning round found he had fallen in. He did not walk in to him, as he did not know the depth of the water, and could not swim, and the ground sloped down there: He got a plank and reached it out under the child, and drew him to land. He was not in the water two minutes. He knew since that the depth of it at that side was about three feet, and on the other side, perhaps five feet. The deceased was in the middle. He lived a good part of half-an-hour after being got out.—lnspector Bowen Would not the water be enough to poison him P—Witness t I don't think it would be far short of that. There is blue waste draining into it. The foreman and another juryman thought Mr. Tildesley might have walked in and saved the boy, but Inspector Bowen said he could not have done so, the ground being so sloping and the child so far off.—The jury returned a verdict that the deceased was acciden- tally drowned. The Coroner could not make any recom- mendation as to the pit, as it was DO yards from the highway.

div.head: RENOVATION OF LATCHFORD BAPTIST
div.p: RENOVATION OF LATCHFORD BAPTIST
CHAPEL.

The Baptist Chapel, Wash-lane, Latchford, is at present undergoing considerable alterations which will materially increase, the comfort of the congre- gation and improve the appearance of the building. The services are at present being held in the adjoin- ing school, which is hardly equal to the demand made upon its accommodation. The architect is Mr. W. Walker, King-st. ; the contractor for the woodwork, Mr. W. Crag,g, of Bewsey-road, and the contractor for the decorations, Mr. Wm. Fletcher, of Suez-st. The old-fashioned high-backed pews have been removed and seating of a more modern char- acter is being substituted, the material of the new pews being pitch pine. A gallery formerly existed across the end of the chapel behind the pulpit, and this has been lowered in the middle, to provide places for the organ and for choir' who have hither- to been accustomed to sit in the front pews. The side galleries will not be required for the congrega- tion at present, and will until it increases be only used on special occasions, when there is a crush. The pulpit has been taken'away and is being super- seded by the rostrum which has found so much 'favour among the Baptist community. A new room is being provided at the back of the chapel which will be used for week evening services, lectures, temperance meetings, and entertainments. A part of the building will be set apart for the communion, there having been previously no such prevision, and within the space, which will be railed off, there will be chairs for the minister and the deacons, and the communion table. The building will be lighted by two handsome twelve-light chandeliers, and ventila- tion is provided for by means of four Tobin's tubes,com- municating with a ventilator on the roof, the warm air from the gas being carried away through the centre tube of the chandelier. The heating pipes, which formerly ran along the aisles, have been transferred to the side walls. In the decoration the ornaments adapted are cen- ventional renderings of Bible fruits and flowers, and are symbolical in their application. The ceiling,4-which was previously a plain, monotonous space, is now broke up into large panels, again cut up into a number of small ones surrounding the sun- lights. The panels are painted a light creamy tint, and enclosed by stiles of a bluish green colour, decided by lines of a russet tint. A margin or the wall colour runs round the entire ceiling, bordered by a dull blue line. The ceiling is supported by a cornice and deep frieze, on which is stencilled in warm blue and russet tints, the pomegranate and vine alternating in a leafy scroll. This is supported by a wave-border in dull blue and red which. also divides the freize from the main part of the we,. The main wall is painted with a light Pompeianred tint, which contrasts harmoniously with the ceiling.. Sup- porting the walls and forming a base to the genera/ colouring is a dado border ten inches deep on.which is stencilled a Tudor rose in dull red and green, on a dark vellum ground. The architraves of the-windows, are painted a warm vellum colour. A stencil border repre- senting the vine leaf runs round the windows. The end wall behind the rostrum is broken into panels.between the windows, two of which contain emblems of the Trinity in colour and gold. The other two panels contain an artistic representation of the lily. The wall under this is diapered with a lily pattern in two shades of the wall colour. On each side of the rostrum the diapering is repeated, and is finished at the top with a quatrefoil freize in red, buff, and gold. The vestrie,s,which are beneath the side galleries, are painted to harmonise with the chapel. The effect is, as a whole, pleasing and harmonious, and aestheticism and comfort will both be ministered to when the metamorphosis the chapel is undergoing is complete. There is now seating accommodation, including the galleries, for about 300 persons. The cost of the alterations is estimated at about £350, about £3OO of wlich has been raised by the bazaar last year, and contributions. The balance, it is expected, will be realised by collections. The re-open- ing services are to be herd; to-morrow week.

THE BACCARAT SCANDAL AND LIBEL ACTION.

In a crowded court, Lord Chief Justice Coleridge, and a special jury on Monday, began the hearing of Sir William Gordon-Cumming's action for slander against Mr. and Mrs. Arthur Wilson, and three other de/endante. The Prince of Wales was present at the opening of the case, but the Solicitor-Genesal„ counsel for the plaintiff, said it was not then known whether his Royal Highness would be called as a witness. Sir William-Gordon Cum- ming wasthe only witness examined on Monday. He stated that in September last he went with the Prince-of Wales toTranby Croft—Mr. Artkur Wilson's residence —for the Doncaster races. Orr the evening of the eth‘ baccarat was played,his Royal Highness acting as banker: The game-was played again on the following night, and the plaintiff won altogether £225. On the evening of the , I,oth plaintiff was informed by General Owen Williams and Lord Coventry that he was accused of cheating at baccarat,and he told them that it was-a foul and abomin- able falsehood. He placed the matter- in the hands of General Owen Williams and Lord Coventry as his friends and they said, after consultation, that the only way of avoiding a horrible scandal would be for him to sign a document in which he was to undertake never to play can& again, and in which they and the- other parties promised to keep the affair secret. Plaintiff protested that this would be like an admission of geilt,hot on their advice, and unde.r their pressure,he signedthe document. He now emphatically denied that there was any truth in the charge that he cheated at baccarat. Ibieross-examin- ationby Sir C. Russell, the plaintiff repeated his denial. He said he"• lost his head "when the accusation was made against him. He thought he was doing a foolish act,but not a dishonourableone, in signing the paper, and he had never ceased to regret it. •

• • TUESDAY:—THE PRINCE OF WALES EXAMINED. On Tuesday the plaintiff was further cross-examined by Sir Charles Russell. Pressed to state why he signed what he admitted was tantamount to an admission of guilt, plaintiff said the thing had become _such public property that he thought it would be taken up by his clubs, his regiments, and his friends. Letters were read in which Sir W. Gordon Cumming acknowledged the friendly disposition shown by General O. Williams and Lord Coventry. When the matter had to come before plaintiff's commanding officer, General Williams author- ised plaintiff) to say that he signed the document men- tioned under•extreme pressure and a promise of secrecy*. The Prince of Wales was next called, and stated that he had been intimate with the plaintiff for twenty years, and travelled down to Tranby Croft on September Bth. On the second evening, after play, Sir W. Gordon Gum- ming showed him his tableau, but nothing had occurred to suggest foul play. The first communication was made to the Prince by Lord Coventry on the evening of the 10th, that statement purporting to come from three gentlemen and: two ladies. A juror asked his Royal Highness whether he himself observed anything suspicious. Tli.s•Prince replied, "No, I did not. We were playing in a country house amongst friends. I was busy acting' as banker, and had no suspicion of such a thing. The charges seemed so unanimous that there was no course open but to believe them." General Owen Williams narrated the circumstances already men- tioned, and said that after the charge was made .Sir William Gordon. Cumming appeared dejected, and said nothing remainedfor him but to vanish or cut his throat. This closed the case for the plaintiff. Describing the scene, on Tuesday, a correspondent says :-,--ThePrinceiwho was dressed in a dark frock coat and wore a blacknecktie, having been sworn, was ques- tioned for nearly a quarter of art hour by the Solicitor. General, and gave his terse replies with peculiar distinct- ness. The cross-examination only occupied ten minutes, characterised by breathless silence. Asked whether he had desired to act leniently out of regard to Sir William,. his Royal Highnessreplied with great emphasis, "Most certainly." Quitea sensation was caused by the almost dramatic close of Sir Charles's questioning, when, on be- ing asked whether he had expressed a wish not to see Sir Gordon Cumming,. the Prince paused, and extending his hands, and with a shrug of the shoulders, answered almost sotto voce-.. "It would be more agreeable not." After a juryman had availed himself of the opportunity to question the Prince of Wales the court adjourned for halt-an-hour, but no. one moved from the gallery, where: sandwiches were brought forth, while many ladies on the bench partook of a-frugal luncheon during the absence of the judge.

div.head: WEDNESDAY.
div.p: WEDNESDAY.

The trial of the baccarat case was resumed on .Wed- nesday, the Prince of Wales being again present. Sir Charles Russell addressed the jury for the defence, argu- ing that plaintiff 4 conduct VMS not that of an innocent man, and that he was content to lie under this serious stigma until he found that he could not slip out of the Army with half-pay, and that the scandal to be avoided by signing the paper was the scandal of being possibly denounced on Doncaster racecourse. Mr. Arthur Wilson, son of the hostws, of Tranby Croft, stated that at the commencement of the first night's play he looked round to see what stakes•were being placed, and noticed a £5, counter on a set note paper in front of Sir William Cumming. When the tableau won he was paid £l5. After that Sir William Cumming looked to see what Lord Edward Somerset had,and on seeing that he had a "natural" and a court card he opened his hand and let drop a£s counter. He was paid £2O, Next time the person drawingthe card drew a very bad one. Sir Wm. Cumming seeingthis, let fall a counter on to his stake. Witness said to his neighbour Levett, "My God, this is too hot ' • this man is cheating." Levett said" Impos- sible." On the second night Lady Coventry had a good card, and plaintiff pushed a £lO counter over the line.. Afterwards,receiving only £s,.plaintiff said to the Prince, "I beg your .pardon, sir, there is another £10." The Prince said, "I wish you would place your stake more conspicuously."

div.head: THURSDAY.
div.p: THURSDAY.

Mr. Wilson,.jisn., in further crrss-examination, stated that the counters used were brought to the house by the Prince of Wales. Witness gave orders for the new bac-- carat table immediately on leaving the room on the Bth. Witness:in his ignorance thought the chalkline that had been drawn made it impossible to cheat. He had absolutely no doubt that he saw cheating as described. He did not challenge it then, because there were ladies present. Mr. Berkeley Levett, Lieut.-Colonel Scots Guards, confirmed the evidence already given, and said that he went after-- wards to. Sir William's private residence by request. Sir William said, "I don't ask you to withdraw; but can't you say you were mistaken ?" Witness ,said, "I must believe my own eyes." Mr. Lycett Green was next examined, and said he at first objected to sign the docu- ment mentioned, but it was pointed out to him that it was an admission by Sir William of guilt. Mrs. Lycett Green stated that on the Bth'the Prince twice said to Sir. William,."-I wish you would place your stake where it- can be seen." The hearing was then adjourned.

div.head: TRAGEDY IN KENTISH TOWN.
div.p: TRAGEDY IN KENTISH TOWN.
DOUBLE MURDER AND SUICIDE.

Information was received at the Kentish Town Police Station on Tuesday morning that a double murder and suicide had been committed at No. 11,,Jeffrey-st.,Kentish Town,. On proceeding_there the police found behind the kitchen door the dead body of a child with its throat frightfully cut. In another part of the house they found the dead body of a man, and in a bedroom on,the second floor the dead body .of a woman. The man and woman also had their throats cut. The man is William Else, a cabdriver, 47, years of age, and the other victims are his wife, Maria Jane Else, a 150.47 years of age* And ' their daughter Alice, aged seven years. From the inquiries that have been made, there is little doubt that the man Else murdered his wife and child, and then cut his own throat, during a fit of temporary insanity caused through anxiety by reason of an accident and loss of work. Until six months ago. he had been in.. good work, but unfortunately about that time he broke a leg and had been unable to work since. During the first three months ha had., been in a convalescent home in London. Recently .he returned, and had since been about on crutches. Be and his wife were both total abstainers, and appeared to be on affectionate terms, but since his illness he has been in a depressed state. He and his wife had three chil- dren, of which the murdered child was the youngest. The eldest, Nellie, is about 13 years of age. She states that her mother had been unwell, and her.-father had been carefully nursing her,, arid sat up with her on Mon- day night. About seven o'cbock on Tuesday inorningher lather came and kissed her, but she saw altnife in his bandiand ran screaming away. She ran downstairs and then found the dead.bodv of her sister Alice. She was unable to do anything, forsome time, ,but as soon as she had recovered somew.hat, from the shcck,she received, she proceeded uustairs,,aral then found the dead bodies of both her father and mother. She then gavean alarm, and the police shortly afterwards arrived.. A,paiñful sen- sation was caused in the neighbourhood, and the street was crowded, with,an excited crowd,until past eleven o'clock, when, the bodies were removed in funerl,l hearses to the Xentish Town mortuary,where the inquest will be held. Jelf7ey-st. is a turning_ out of Kentish Town-road,, and ia the next street to Priory-st., where Mrs. Pearcey murdered Mrs. Phcsbe.Hogg and her infant child.

div.head: INQUEST.
div.p: THE INQUEST.

On Wednesday, at St. Pan-craii,-,t-lie coroner, Dr. Dan,- ford Thomas, held an inquest on the, body of William Else, author of Tuesday's Kentish Town tragedy, and also of Maria Jane Else, wile, and Alice Else, daughter, his victims. Dr. Robert Milne Beaton deescribed all the wounds as of a shocking nature, wending from ear to ear, and going back to the spine. The jury found that Esc, while of unsound mind, had murdered his Naffs, and child, and then committed suicide. -
