THE EDDISBURY DIVISION.-A LIBERAL CANDIDATE.

A large and representative meeting of Liberal delegates from the various polling districts in the Eddisbury Division of Cheshire was held at the Temperance Hall, Chester, on Saturday, for the pur- pose of choosing a candidate. The reports from the different districts were highly encouraging, and it was stated that the ',arty organisation was never in better condition. Mr. James Tomkinson, who unsuccessifully contested the seat on the last occa- sion against Mr. Henry Tollemache, the sitting Con- servative member, delivered an interesting speech on the situation, and was enthusiastically received. A resolution adopting Mr. Tomkinson as the Liberal candidate was unanimously passed. •
ALLEGED CRIMINAL LIBEL ON A WARRINGTON SOLICITOR.
DEFENDANT COMMITTED FOR TRIAL.

At the Warrington Borough Police Court, on Monday. before the Mayor (Alderman R. W. Fran- Comb) in the chair, and Alderman Harrison, John -Warburton, formerly of Calland's Farm, Burton- wood, and now residing in Lovely-lane, Warrington, an independent gentleman, was charged with un- lawfully writing and publishing certain libels against William Henry Jenkins, of the firm of Jenkins and Unsworth, solicitors, Winwick-straet, 'Warrington. and residing at Orchard Gottage, rad- gate. Mr. Unsworth, the prosecutor's partner, ap- peared for the prosecution, and Mr. A. Browne for the defendant who occupied a seat next to his soli- tor.--Mr. Unsworth in opening the proceedings aaid the defendant was separated from his wife, and having given up farming had nothing to do to ' occupy his time with, which seemed rather a pity, because the devil always found something for a man to do under such circumstances.—Mr. Browne objected to such remarks as uncalled for, and irrelevant, and, in the course of some conversation on the matter, the Mayor reinarked to Mr. Browne : I thought you were objecting to the old gentleman finding Mr. Warburton something to do. (Laughter.)—lt was finally ruled that Mr. Uns- Worth was quite in order, and he proceeded to say that at the last Winter-Assizes—Mr.Browne objected to this as irrelevant.—Thedeputy Magistrates' Clerk said it had nothing to do with the case, but they could allow this.— The Chairman (to Mr. Unsworth) : I don't think you need go back to that.—Mr. Unsworth said it was a Matter of public notoriety. The prosecutor since then had given the defendant every opportunity to desist from publishing these libels, and had gone so far as to 'Write to his solicitcrs in Liverpool asking them to try to stop him from . circulating them. Mr. Uns- Worth was about to read the letter sent to them when Mr. Browne objected that the letter had nothing to do With the present case. Mr. Unsworth was allowed to lead the correspondence. He read a letter sent by his aril to the defendant's solicitors requesting them to use their influence with him to induce him to conduct him- :self with something like decency, as he;persisted in mak- ing the most filthy and untruthful charges against Mr. venkirle. If the practice were not stopped steps would • •Ve to be taken to put a stop to the nuisance. Mr. utisworth then read a reply from the defendant's solici- tors expressing regret that Mr. Jenkins still suffered from the annoyance, and promising to speak to Mr. Warbur- t°,ri very seriously on the matter. After this letter, Mr. unsworth said the defendant continued to issue his libellous publications. Mr. Jenkins, however, took no steps until he received a posteard dated May 26th last, Which was the first libel now complained of. Other two `L'arges as to the 6th of May were incorporated in one gommons, and the postcards in these two cases were ad- dressed Wm. Henry Jenkins, alias Brierley, No. 1, Bank Phambers, Winwick-st., Warrington. The alias was in itself a serious libel, and the name Brierley was used by 11e defendant in connec,tion with a song which he pub- Ished called "Driven from home" which was a subject action at the Assizes.—Alderman Harrison: Is it a reference to the Brierley who had connection with Mrs. ~,aYbrick's business P—Mr. Unsworth said that was so. :Lob prosecutor waited as long as hs possibly could, in 7_le hope that the defendant would desist, at 115 felt obliged to bring the matter before their wor- TIPs and ask them to commit the defendant for trial at ;:fle Assizes.—Mr. Jenkins deposed to the receipt of a libellous postcard on the 7th of May, dated the 6'll, in the defendant's handwriting. After that he received !Mother in defendant's handwriting—it might have been the following day—handed him by Mr.Hewitt,veterinary aUrgeon.—Mr. Browne: We are not responsible for the publication by a third party, even supposing my client bad written it.—Mr. Unsworth : It has been held that the mere fact of a card going through the Post Office Mast of necessity be publication.—Mr. Browne: Where You can have primary evidence you cannot produce seo oridary. You must prove it was received by the per- son to whom it was addressed.—Mr. Jenkins: Mr. Hewitt promised to be here, but he is suddenly called away. We will bring him to the Assizes.—The complain- ant said the handwriting on the card was the defend- ant's without any disguise.—Mr. Unsworth proposed to Put in a letter from tke defendant,which was not a libel, to prove his handwriting. That letter had been admitted ry the defendant's counsel at the Liverpool Assizes to be '4 his client's writing.—Mr. Browne objected to the let- ter being put in.—Mr. Jenkins Rather than this should go on, and I should be annoyed persistently, there are !tiler charges which I shall certainly prefer. I shall not g'a thwarted. Either I will crush him or he shall crush !tee There shall be no half measures about it. I will Put a stop to it once for all.—The complainant, further t▪ olined,said he received the letter produced,dated May 1,:,"1,1889. He might say there were much more serious :vets than those he now complained of. The letter was Zghed by the defendant himself, and brought to him by defendant. There was not the slightest truth in the sbarge that witness was known as Brierley by anyone aer, Pt the defendant. Witness had been acting as wor for the defendant's wife for a long time. She „t.)Now living apart from him in consequence of pro- ise'"„ logs brought by witness on herbelialf. He accepted : I.°flainal verdict for £2O in Dee. last, as damages in waspect of libels by the defendant. The term Brierley ii`„been applied to him by the defendant in hundreds of sh-'Dos publications.—This ended the first case, though Was another indictment against the defendant. Mr. egyne asked for an adjournment of the proceedings for tee:ll days, as he had been entirely unaware of the con- e,: of the alleged libellous communications until he 131;"eto court that morning, and consequently would be •,,,,rlced at a disadvantage if he had not time to consider jsual Course to take in the matter. He would like an ad- sub".unlent in order that he might take advice on the IlsoLect•—Alderman Harrison: You mean to say, Mr. that you have been taken by surprise P—Mr. thaine replied that he could not say that, but admitted of he did not think the communications complained nrarere anything like what they were. His client in- havu,,,,,teci him he did not know a word about them, not adir,-„-g written them.—Mr. Unsworth objected to an tirw"roinent as not likely to be of any advantage to Mr. thc„,wne• The third card was .a great deal worse than krlalready put in.—The Bench decided to proceed.— . 'Jenkins then deposed to receiving on the 27th of feeYd knottier libellous card dated the 26th, from the de- she n his handwriting,slightly disguised. None of Alice Statements contained on the card were true.—Miss deliv Jenny Meeks, postal messenger at Padgate, said she iti._red the card at the defendant's house to Mr. A. J. k thno• She read the address on it, but did not know what ni Brierley referred to. She had heard of it before. „:!Srthur Joseph Martin, employed by Mr. Jenkins, de- r_sfd to receiving the card from Miss Meeks and hand- it to his entployer.—Mr. Browne, who had reserved no.,:cross examination, now said, that in the cases of Te.,libels, their truth might be preyed, but in a case the present there were such a conglomeration and a:fa of different kinds of libels that it would be impos- Zu_le to prove the truth of them all. Therefore he nt.ilight their worships might see their way clear to an s to see if anything could be %tiieurnment for seven day done between the parties without prejudice to any further proceedings.—Alderman Harrison: I presume 70ur client has seen this ?—Mr. Browne. I have shown it to him.—Alderman Harrison: And he does not deny it S—Mr. Browne: I don't admit it, sir.—Mr. Unsworth said he could quite understand Mr. ernowtnoe'tshheopreosctehetg I,lDinotiting might be done to put an. B d Ns, but his (Mr. Jenkins's) life had been so I?arrassed "Y this man during the past 15 months that he was 6,w):lliged to take very stringent measures, and nothing t2Loid._ satisfy him other than allowing the law to 1;;;:r I.ts course. It would be nerfectly useless attempt- _to approach him in any manner whatever. tr4owiagman Harrison .said he fully realised that Mr. ad,„,„ was in a difficult position.—Mr. Browne ),flitted that he was placed in such a position . the Jenkins: I am charged with immorality of of tresest possible description, and I challenge proof half 11,.eharges.—Mr. Browne pleaded not guilty, on be- send'i'Lt his client, and reserved his defence ; and the'de- Vhietillt7 Was committed for trial at Liverpool Assizes, as so commence on July 25th. I discussion took place ac__ the amount of bail to be required from him, the thl'evoptaoce of bail being compulsory in such cases. Mr. that .rth pressed for heavy bail.—Mr. Browne stated burtosiaix, months since a friend offered to pay Mr. War- roue,, a expenses if he would accompany him on a tour ChiLd the world, and he declined to leave his wife and eoneteor!•,,, Therefore he was not likely to abscond on ac- the tief L mese proceedings.—The Bench decided to accept BOreticeendant's own recognisances for £lOO, and two ler £25 each.

It Is in the neighbourhood of" " Seville, that the orauges best suited for " "marmalade making are grewn. A recent" "frost (the like of wh;eh has not been ex-" " perienced for ten years), __,,llayed havoc" " with the fruit, and, although though the" full extent of the damage is not yet" known, it is believed that fully one half " the orange crop has been destroyed." Ertters to the &dor.
THE LATE MR. BRADLAUGII.

Sir,—l learn from Mr. Holyoake that a fund is being raised for redeeming Mr. Bradlaugh's property, in order to make some provision for his only surviving daughter, airs. Bonner, who, at a time of great pecuniary embar- rassment, sacrificed on her father's behalf the life policy he had assigned to her. Hundreds of kindly notices and regrets for the harsh treatment Mr. Bradlaugh received have appeared recently in the newspapers ; we have now p:ove that these words were no mere empty senti- ment to relieve our own sense of discomfort, but genuine, unselfish sympathy. The debts which Mr. Bradlaugh left were not selfish debts, for he lived in poverty, and till the last seven years had not been known to take so much as a week'sholiday. It was the enormous amount of litigation forced upon him—especially during the Parliamentary struggle—which involved him in these expenses, and had he lived a few years longer he would .have been able to meet them. Some of the creditors have reduced their claims, so that if a sum of £3,000 can now be raised the debts could be settled, and the difficulty ot Mrs. Bonner's position in some degree lessened. The Souse of Commons, by expunging from its journals the resolution which refused Mr. Bradlaugh the right to take his seat, has done a little to make up for the grave in- justice of the past But our individual responsibility remains. May we not make some slight amends by expunging from our hearts all fear of being •misunderstood, and by showing justice and gene- rosity now? Though writing always on the Chris- tian side, I received from Mr. Bradlaugh great courtesy and 'kindness, and I feel very strongly that many who regret the intolerance which had for him such serious re- sults will be glad to find there still remains something that they may do in this matter. If every Lib3ral had the courage of his convictions and subscribed to this fund I venture to think it would be a bit of practical Chris- tianity, as well as a fitting tribute to a man whose integ- rity has been acknowledged even by his opponents, and who died in his prime, worn out with toil, yet to the last thinking of others' needs. Subscriptions should be sent at once to George Ander- son, Esq., 35, Great George-st., Westmin§ter. S.W.— Yours, &c., EDNA LYALL. (Ada Ellen Bayly.)

div.head: APOSTOLIC SUCCESSION, &c.
div.p: APOSTOLIC SUCCESSION, &c.

Sir,—As some of your many readers may think I gave too brief an outline in4ny last, with your kind permis- sion I would say the Douay Bible with Haydock's notes says "The word baptism signifies a washing particularly when it is done by immersion, or by dipping or plunging a thing under water which was formerly the ordinary way of administering the sacrament of baptism. That Christ was baptized by immersion is clear from the text, For he that ascended nut of the water must first have de- scended into it. And this method was in general use in the church for 130ayear5, as appears from the acts of councils and ancient rituals." Dean Stanley confirms this.

Benjamin Keach wrote: When one is baptized, he ought to be covered all over with water, or else it is no baptism. W. Smith D.C.L. in his Bible Dictionary, a standard work says. There is no mention of infaut baptism or sponsors in the New Testament. Neander says," It cannot possibly be proved that in- fant baptism was practised in the Apostolic age." Bap- tism, in the Scriptural sense of the term, considered as the Christian initiatory ordinance, is putting a believer under water. Note a believer not an infant incapable of repentence and faith or being able to exclaim "I believe."

Dean Alford says, " It is not by successive delegation from the Apostles of which fiction I find no trace in the New Testament." The Church of England speaks out most strongly against this popish doctrine in her article 35 the Homily for Whit-Sunday, alas how many of the clergy assent and consent to these articles merely to get the Loaves and fishes, then ignore them. _

Bishop J. B. Lightfoot says the functions of theapog- ties and bishops differed widely. The apostle, like the prophet or evangelist, held no local office. He was es- sentially as the name denotes, a missionary, moving about from place to place, founding and confirming new brotherhoods. Alex. Hyslop, in is "Two Babvlons," a book worthy of a place in every library. says : " Aposto- lic men for the laying of the foundations of the Christian Church, were by their great King and Head, invested with miraculous powers—powers which were intended only for a time, and were destined,as the Apostles them- selves declared, while exercising them, to vanish away." 1 Cor. 13c. Bv. Sir R. Phayre says :t" Them which call themselves Apostles are not, the Apostles have no suc- cessors." The Rev. Enoch Mellor said: "The Apostles could have no successors." Between A.D. 1135 and 1154 there were two rival Archbishops of York. Archbishop Tillotson was brought up a Baptist, and there is no re- cord of his ever being baptised or sprinkled. It is upon Peter's confession "Thou art Christ, the Son of the living God," that the Church was to be built, not upon Peter himself. Other foundation says Paul "could no man lay," &c., 1 Cor. 3c. 11v. Frodsham, June, 1891.
ROBERT FOULKES.

div.head: STATE PRIESTISNI : SOME STRANGE CONTRASTS.
div.p: STATE PRIESTISNI : SOME STRANGE CONTRASTS.

Sir,—Kindly permit me to resume my remarks on this subject. 4. When Jesus had arrived at the age of thirty years, he left his retirement in the hills of Galilee, and was bap- tised by his forerunner John in the river Jordan, in the presence of a vast concourse of his fellow countrymen gathered together from all parts. Now, if his idea of baptism had been analogous to the one that now gener- ally prevails he might have saved himself from a toil- some and lonely journey of some eighty miles on foot, and from the curious gaze of a motley and perhaps un- sympathetic crowd by being duly sprinkled and crossed by some rabbi in a synagogue in his native town. But baptism was in his estimation, a very solemn thing indeed; not a meaningless ceremony for babies, but a manly and open renunciation of the world, and the beginning of a new and heavenly life to be devoted to the service of God and man. His immersion in the waters of Jordan, was the initial step of his great mis- sion, and his first public taking up of that cross of humi- liation, poverty, and persecution which he only laid down with his life at Calvary. And before ascending up into heaven he gave commandment to the apostles and, through them, to his church in all ages, to preach his gospel, and baptise his disciples. Rut who ever heard of a prelate teing so baptised ! No English river has ever had the higo honour of bathing the sacred persons of the reverend fathers in that holy rite. How could men so delicately nurtured, and so valuable to mankind, be expected to risk their health and comfort by immer- tion in the cold and muddy waters of our northern clinic —even in obedience to a Divine command! To the fashionable world of religionists the spectacle of a bi- shop in such circumstances would be no small scandal, and profane sightseers might be inclined to mock the proceedings. But the reverend fathers must, of ccurse, be loyal to the Master whose apostles they profess to be, and they show their attachments and obedience by quietly setting aside his ordinance for a figment of their own invention. This figment involves no trouble, no risk, and no persecution, and has the additional advant- age of being highly popular with modern Christians from the Pope downwards. The invention may bear no - to the believers' baptism prac- tised and enjoinea by Jesus Mill Llta ailvousc,, niuto according to the dictum of "the Church," it produces most wonderful results, inasmuch as it instantaneously transforms the children of men into " Members of Christ, children of God, and inheritors of the Kingdom of Heaven." With such powers at their finger ends we may well be astonished that there are so few real Christians to be found even in this favoured land. 5. In the matter of dress, we have no intimation in the new Testament that Jesus differed in any way from the lowly people with whom he associated. The sacred records only mention one article of his clothing, namely, the coat for which the Roman soldiers cast lots at his crucifixion, and the only peculiarity about it was that it was woven throughout without seams. The great Teactier had no need to adorn himself with the gaudy ' trappings of the world in order to secure popular atten- tion ; and we feel assured that it never entered into His mind to glorify His Father by a display of millinery. It was the beauty of his countenance irradiated by the light and glory of a pure and sinless life, and the Divine power of his word and works that gathered multitudes around Him whenever he appeared in public. But in their garments. as well as in other things, the reverend fathers have a peculiar way of showing obedience to their Master's example. Lowliness of mind, and plainness of attire may suit the common people, but these simple virtues do not commend themselves to the episcopal mind. High and learned men, as the fathers are said be must have some distinguishing marks about them ; and, as they possess no special graces, they can, at any rate, lay claim to special clothing. Hence we find them array- ing themselves in mitres, breeches, gaiters, gowns, and other kindred ecclesiastical toggery. What connection these things can have with the occupation of men who profess to win souls for Christ I have never been able to liscover ; and lam equally at a loss to understand how they can be otherwise than dishonouring to Him who in His life and teaching inculcated thedeepest humility, and abstention from the pomps and vanities of the world. But viewed from another point, I am constrained to confess that the priestly vestments are not without their uses. As liveries of the State, they indicate plainly whose servants the reverend fathers are, and at the same time give a showy prominence to men who would otherwise be little known or cared for beyond their own immediate circles. _

.When Jesus commenced his ministry, he did not consider it necessary to have titles added to his name in order that he might thereby be distinguished from other men, and receive the servile homage of the religious Com- munity. To be known amongst his countrymen as Jesus of Nazareth, the carpenter, was enough for him. He had come into the world to fill a glorious, yet lowly, place, and to be poor that we through his poverty, might be made rich, and therefore could have nothing Whatever to do with the vain conceits with which poor human nature loves to adorn itself. His object on earth was the glory of God, and the salvation of men, and not masquer- ading in priestly habiliments. But his was an age of darkness, ours is one of great light and knowledge, and so our ecclesiastics have discovered a wonderful way of imitating his humility. Directly a man has obtained his trade union diploma for " ministering " in "the church" he is launched upon the people as a reverend gentleman, that is a man worthy to bear a name which the Scrip- tures apply to God, and to him alone! This piece cf clerical irmpudence and irreverence is surely bad enough; but it is completely thrown into the shade by the daring impiety of the Bishops. Not content with bring styled reverend masters in arts, doctors in divinity, &c., they must needs flaunt themselves before us as right reverend, and most reverend fathers in God, Lord Bishops of so and so! This is the way in which the Bishops honour the command of Jesus, " Be ye not called Rabbi : for one is your master, even Christ ; and all we are brethren. And call no man your father upon the earth ; for one is your father which is in heaven !" Well may we say of them as Jesus said of their prototypes the scribes and pharisees of his day, " How can ye believe, which receive honour one of another, and seek not the honour that cometh from God only." I have not yet exhausted my subject, but with your kind permission, I hope to conclude in a third letter.— Yours faithfully, lONA.

div.head: .LrAlli.
div.p: .LrAlli.

CYCLtsTs AND THE FOOTPATUS.—LateIy there have been many complaints in Lymm and the surrounding district of children having been knocked down by cyclists riding on the footpaths. So on Saturday, when a num- ber of cyclists belonging to a Lancashire club, were caught by a policeman riding in Indian file ona footpath near Lymm, they were stopped and questioned, and will be summoned at the next Petty Sessions. DEATH OF Ma. W. C. BOWEN.—The announcement of the death of .Mr. W. C. Bowen, Booth's-hill, was received in Lymm with much regret. The deceased gentleman had been for about two years in very delicate health ,and when, latterly, he was attacked by pneumonia his en- feebled frame was unable to withstand this fresh assault, and he died on the 29th May. The deceased gentleman had been a resident of Lymm for about 16 years,and was a member of the Congregational Church. He was also a member of the Liberal Club, and until recently took a very aetive part in political matters. Mr. Bliwen was 66 years of age,and leaves a widow and family to mourn his loss. The funeral took place on Monday, time last resting-place of the deceased being St. Phillip's Park Cemetery, Bradford, near Manchester. Many beautiful wreaths were sent by friends.
The bank rate of discount is reduced from 5 to 4 per cent.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 6, 1891.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 6, 1891.
"EAWIt BASHAW !"

A FAMILY DITI T. Mi feyther browt up tharteen lads, Wi'th' Prayer Book an' a stick; An' tho' he hommert us to mitch, He wur a good owd brick. uset to sheawt at baggin' time. "Come reawnd me, greyt an' sma' ; Tore aw inclined for divilment, But Bashaw byets yo' aw ! " Eawr Hurman wur a sarious lad, An' workt upo' this plan He savet his brass, an' ev'ry year He went to' tlf Isle of Man. Ov late th' owd scholar hezn't bin—
Ther'ssummut wrung, shuz heaw; For, tho' he's fond o' wayter, yet He never sails noan neaw ! Eawr Izuk's yungst, or, what we caw The ritlin' in eawr parts; He wur ml mother's favourite—
Her preshus King o' Hearts. He uset to play at sojerin', Wur " A I " wi' a gun - But when we seed him I;okin' it,

• We allus cut an' run! Eawr.Yethart's gam' wur coortin',— The wimmin wur his taste; lie liket sum wee] to hey his arm Clipt reawnd a slender waist. An' Dick too, wur a clicer yeauth, An' bored his yed wi' books; But, strange to say, he ne'er cud tell Owd carron crows fro' rooks! Eawr Charlie studied langwidges Pro' ey'ry forrin' loud; An' sung such sungs, az not Owd Nick Hisser cud understond. While Jack, "Mad Jack," wur alias deawn On parsons an' collekshuns; An' never tiret o' showin' up Ther cadgin' imperfecshuus. 'Twud tak' to lung to write abeawt The rest o' eawr rum crew; A wole newspapper cud be filled, An' ey'ry word on't true. But, az mi feyther allus sed,— " He may be rayther raw, But for playin' bows an' crackin' jokes, Eawr Bashaw byets yo aw !" _ TUM 0' PEGS. .

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday, under the presidency of Mr. Mclntyre. Present: Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Knowles, (vice-chairman), P. Speakman, C.C., S. Taylor, E. Aaron. J. Stokes, J. Baguley, T. Lea, Elli- son, Baxter, Pickering, Wilkinson, Hewitt, Bran- dreth, J. Whitlow, W. Whitlow, J. W. Baguley, and 11. G. Linaker, (acting clerk). THE ADMINISTRATION OF OUTDOOR EHLIEF.

In accordance with notice he had given,Mr. Speakman moved that the resolution adopting the regulations passed at the conference on outdoor relief at Northwick be rescinded.— Mr. Stokes seconded. Carried. Mr. Aaron then moved the adoption of the following regulations for out door relief.—l. Out- door relief shill not in future be granted (except in case of sickness) to applicants of any of the following classes :—(a) single able-bodied men ; (b) single able- bodied women ; (c)able-bodied widows without children, or having only one child to support; (d) married wotnen (with or without families),whose husbands hav- ing been convicted of crime, are undergoing a term of imprisonment; (e) married women (with or without families), deserted by their husbands ; (f) persons resid- ing with relatives,where the united income of the family is sufficient for the support of all its members, whether such relatives are liable by law to support the applicant or not; (g) non-residents. 11. Out-door relief shall not be granted in any case for a longer period than thir- teen weeks at a time. 111. Out-door relief shall not be granted on account of the sickness of the applicant, or any of his family, for a longer period than two weeks at a time unless such sickness shall be certified in writing by the District Medical Officer, as being likely to be of long duration, and then only for a fixed period. IV. As far as possible the use of wino, spirits, and beer, as Medical Extras for out-door paupers shall be discontinued. V. Out-door relief shall not be granted to widows who, on the death of their husbands,have received money from a club, insurance society, or other source, which, in the opinion of the Relief Committee or the Board, has been lavishly spent in mourning or funeral expenses, or has been otherwise improperly expended, until the ex- piration of at least one month from the death of their husbands. VI. That sick money received from a club by an applicant for relief shall be taken at the full value. VII. That no medical extras be allowed unless the ap- p:ication be accompanied by a report from the Medical Officer setting forth the particular nature of the disease, the article ordered, and the period for which the recom- mendation is made. That every recommendation made by the Medical Officer be brought up at the next meetiug of the Board for examination, consideration, and deci- sion. VIII. That the maximum scale of relief for adults be 3s. each person, and that the scale of relief for widows with children be is. 6d. for each child after the first. IX. That in any special case in which it may be pro- posed to deviate from these rules the proposal be brought before the whole Board for consideration and determina- tion.—Mr. Whitlow seconded the motion.—ln reply to questions, Mr. Aaron said these regulatiens were only intended to apply to new cases.—Mr. Speakman said he thought clause D would be a positive hardship.—The Chairman said those who had studied the question thought it would act as a deterrent from crime.—Mr. Taylor pointed out that by clause nine the Board could give out-door relief when the circumstances were such that the woman deserved it.—After some discussion, the clauses were approved by a large majority.
THE COUNTY RATE.-IMPORTANT EXPLANATION.

Thc Clerk then presented his comparative statement, which had been prepared with a view to show the cause of the increase of the poor-rate. The total amount of salaries paid by the Union was £2,123 us. id. and £B2 is. 2d. for superannuation. There had been no increase in the salaries; in fact they were less than they were ten years ago. The cost of indoor relief had been in 1888, £1,272 9s. 7d ; 1889, £1,262 9s. lid; 1890, £1,123 Os. 10d. ; half year ending March 1891, £592. Outdoor relief had been 1888, £3,914 6s. 4d. ; 1889, £3,834 15s. ; 1890, £3,858 18s. id.; and half year ending March 1891, £1,765. The payment to non-resident poor which was out-door relief was ;-1888, £5 25.; 1889, £4l Bs. 101; 1890, £49 Bs. 3d. Lunatics had cost :-1888, £7OO 9s. lid.; 1889, £735 18s. 3d.; 1890, £734 15s. 9d.; half year ending March 1891, £3Bl.—Mr. Brandreth : They vary very little.—The Clerk : There is no appreci- able difference.—Mr. Aaron: There is nothing for it but County Council.—The Clerk : Now for the county t;e'tler ictja" v r . LAT!Sme peakman s 2 hadid in 1881 the county call was £4,452 Ibbs. ; 1885, £1,134 is. 7d. ; 1888, £3.987 4s. 101 ; 1887, £4,486 14s. 2d. ; 1888, £3,898 ss. 3d. ; 1889, £3,552 3s. ; 1890,£7,258 16s. —Dr. Gastaldi : Well done, County Council.—The Clerk said for Lady Day half-year of 1891 the call was £3,126 us. 9d., so that it would be somewhere near £7,000 for this year. He thought that explained the in- crease in the rates, with the exception of some town- ships which had a balance on the wrong side.—The Chair- man : That looks as if we were bringing it home to the C. C. Perhaps Mr.Speakman will be able to give a little ex- , planation.—Mr. Stokes said in Halton the rate had been doubled, and was now at is. Bd. in the £.—The Clerk said there was a balance against that township in Sep- tember.—Mr. Speakman said it would appear by merely talc:ng the several amounts at which the county rate had been levied during the past three years, that there was some excuse for the opinion that the management of the county was a more costly matter under the County Council than it was under the magistrates. If the circumstances were closely looked into, it would be seen that such was not the fact, but that the work was managed quite as economically, if not more so than when it was per- formed by the magistrates, notwithstanding that the wok of the County Council had been increased more than fourfold, and was very much more complicated land in many respects more important. During many years past whilst the county business was managed by the magistrates, the county rate was never lower than 3d. in the £, and very often 4d, in the £ and in the year 1872 was Rd. in the £, notwithstanding that in that year the River Weaver paid a grant to the county. The rates levied by the County Council had only been to meet actual expenditure. When the County Council came in- to existence on Ist April. 1889, there were liabilities out- standing of quite £26,000, and the usual county rate of the preceding January was unlevied by the magistrates. The County Council had also to provide for the total cost of main roads as well as for new items of expenditure,such as costs of County Council elections and other matters not heard of under the magistrates. The result of all this was that the Council had at once to provide a rate of 61d in the £ or double what it had been in the previous year. The following year the County Council felt the benefit of having boldly met its liabilities,and the county rate then fell to 3-Id. in the £ notwithstanding the large ex- penditure on the main roads, and that the usual monies (£lO,OOO or £15,000), frail the River Weaver had not been received. The present year's estimate brought the County rate up to Sd. in the £, in order to meet the growth- of expenditure on main roads and the loss of revenue from the River Weaver and many new matters. But as the 'relief was given to highway authorities, whether rural or urban, there should be a very considerable decrease in the local highway rates of the county. Formerly the county charge for main roads was about £20,000 per annum, and they got about £lO,OOO back from the Government. Now the estimated county charge for main roads was about £60,000 per annum, and they estimated to receive about £37,000 per annum back from the exchequer fund, which the Gov- ernment now handed over to the County Council to ad- minister themselves, and it was estimated that for this year there would be £37,000 as a surplus after the County had paid all the grants due out of the account, and but for this fact the County rate would be nd. more in the -2 than it was. It was estimated that there would be received from Government this year,about £90,000, and the Council would have to make all the grants chargeable thereon and then pay the balance over to its own credit in aid of the County rate,which practically meant in aid of main roads. One of the grants paid by the County was the new grant for the cost of Union officers,and the Unions would benefit to over £15,000 per annum by this. So that in truth it was not the County Council which was most expensive but the fact that it had greater liabilities to meet. The highway and local boards should,however, show a considerable reduction in the expenditure equal at least te 2d, in the £, and the Unions should also show a reduction in their expenditure to the above £15,000 for costs ot union officers. In con- clusion, notwithstanding the cattle plague debt, Cheshire had one of the smallest debts in the country, and if no new loans were raised by the year 1900 the debt would be less than £lO,OOO, which in itself, would reduce the county rate by 1/d. in the £.—ln reply to a question, the Clerk said last year the union received £1,416 from the Coninty Council on account of the union officers That still left the county rate £5,842,an increase of about £1,300 on the previous year.—Mr. Aaron said the money was going in this way: There was a surveyor at £9OO a year and four others at £2OO a year, and in spite of all this extra expense by the Council, not one penny had been saved to Daresbury Highway Board.—Mr. Baxter said there were two sets of men, and they had to travel over each ether's lengths.—Mr. Speakman said the roads in the rural districts had been neglected. The Council would not take over any road that was not put in good I order. The question'of the surveyors had been carefully considered and they were necessary for the proper administration of the highways of the county.—Mr. Whitlow said it would boa good thing to place the main roads in the contr -A of the local highway board again .- 1 The discussion then dropped.

THE PARK.

On Monday evening a meeting was held of the Committee appointed to form the Park Company. There was a good attendance. The memorandum of agreement and the articles of association were signed by the original subscribers. Immediate steps are to be taken to have the company registered and put on a proper basis.

div.head: BRITISH. AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.
div.p: BRITISH. AND FOREIGN BIBLE SOCIETY.

On Thursday evening the annual meeting of the above society was held in the Wesleyan day school. There was a large attendance, and the chair was occupied by Mr. R. Garnett. The Rev. Jelinger E. Symons gave an interesting account of the Bible Society's doings in connection with the African Missions.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C. BY AN OCCASIONAL COILICESPONDENT.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN, &C. BY AN OCCASIONAL COILICESPONDENT.

The declaration of Dr. McDougall to the Board of Commissioners that the severity of the influenza epidemic was abated, and that, in fact, the "in- fluenza wave" was passing away from the district, will be hailed with great satisfaction. High and low, rich and poor, have been within its dread grip,' and on Thursday Mr. J. W. Lightburn was unable to be present at the meeting, and Mr. E. Marshall, the secretary, is incapacitated from fulfilling his duties through an attack of the disease. The re- from the cause during May is a very heavy one. A deputation from Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners, consisting of Mr. S. Taylor, the Chairman, Mr. F. Wiswall, and the Law Clerk (Mr. F. A.Lake) waited upon the General Purposes Committee of the Widnes Local Board, on Wednesday, with res- pect to the suggested bridge across the Mersey for vehicular traffic. The inadequacy of the present means of communication between tt e shores of the bfersey at Widnes and Runcorn needed no demon- stration, while the great benefits which must accrue to those two towns and the surrounding district from the construction of a cartway across the river, only needed pointing out to be recognised and admitted. The deputation sug- gested that the respective local authorities should endeavour to get the County Councils of Lanca,hire and Cheshire to move in the matter. Mr. E. Brown, chairman, on behalf of Widnes Local Board assured the deputation that they would help the project by all means in their power. At the same time, as one visiting the Lancashire side, I must say there is a little jealousy amongst Widnesians on the matter. Although the Runcorn Board of Guardians came to no resolution with regard ta the county rate on Tuesday, and indeed it is difficult to see to what conclusion they could arrive, the discussion will have done much good. It has put the ratepayers in possession of valuable information with regard to the cost of the union and the manner in which the County Council view the financial condition of the county. Mr. Speak- man's contribution to the discussion was a most valuable one.

It would seem that the chief economy could be effected in the administration of the main roads. It would appear that a great saving of money might be effected if the County would either take over the whole of the county roads and dispense with the highway boards altogether or allow the highway boards to repair the whole of the roads in their respective districts. The distribution of prizes to the successful students of the evening classes at Greenway-road Board School on Wednesday night was a very pleas- ing function, and Dr. McDotzgall,who officiated,gave some good advice to the boys. The success of the classes, especially considering that it was the initial attempt, has been phenomenal, and much of it is due to the steady and persistent labours of Mr. Moulton, the headmaster.

div.head: BURSTING OF A WATER MAIN AT ST.
div.p: BURSTING OF A WATER MAIN AT ST.
HELENS.

On Saturday afternoon the workmen employed by the water department of the Liverpool Corpora- tion completed repairs of a portion of the large water main from Rivington to Prescot, where a serious fracture was discovered earlier in the week. The Liverpool Corporation pipes from Rivington pass through a part of the borough of St. Helens and on to the storage reservoirs at Prescot. The entire route is traversed daily by water men in the em- ploy of the Corporation, and while this work was being done on Wednesday week it was discovered that water was issuing in considerable volume from what is known as Yates's Field, behind Eccleston Grange, the residence of Alderman D. M'Kechnie, J.P. on the summit of Eccleston Hill and just on the outskirts of St. Helens. An examination of the spot revealed the fact that from some cause an immense quantity of water was escaping from the mains, and the matter was at once reported to the head office at Liverpool. A gang of Corporation work- men arrived from Liverpool, and they set to work to repair the leakage. The water, in the meantime, rushed down the centre of the field, across the next field, and into a small water course which runs through Eccleston Orders were despatched for the Rivington supply to be turned off at Montrey Flail, near Garswood, some half a dozen miles away, and the water which ran to waste was the immense quantity contained in the pipes for that dis- tance, and the additional quantity which passed through before the orders could be carried into effect. The exca- vations by the workmen showed that one of the lengths of iron piping, about an inch in thickness, had given way at the bottom,leaving a wide fracture through which the water continued to pour. When the outflow had , ceased on 'Thursday the burst pipe was removed,and the work of inserting a new length was completed, as stated on Saturday. The supply from Rivington was again , turned on about three o'clock in the afternoon. The iron was littleover an inch in thickness and the pipe 44 inches in diameter. Like the rest of the Rivington water main it was laid down prior to 1857, in which year the water from Rivington was first turned on. The quantity of water passing through the pipes is estimated at twelve and a half million gallons per day, and the Prescot reser- voirs are situated about a mile from the spot whet e the breakage occurred. Fortunately, the bursting of the main occasioned very little damage to property owing to the water course in the immediate vicinity. At Eccles- ton-hill the main pipes lie about nine fed from the sur- face of the ground.

The poor man was convesed home, and was attended by Dr. Brindle,

div.p: TECHNICAL EDUCATION.

It w!ll be seen from an advertisement in another column that the Technical Instruction Committee of the Corporation is prepared to receive applica- tions for qualified teachers in various subjects for the session 1891-92. Music IN THE PARE.

On Sunday afternoon the hand stand in the Park was occupied by the band of the first Volunteer Battalion (Prince of Wales') South Lancashire Regi- ment, under the direction of Bandmaster Armstrong. This was the first of the organized performances which are to be given during the season. The weather was pleasant, and the attendance was large.

div.head: PICNIC TO CHESTER.
div.p: PICNIC TO CHESTER.

Mr. J. Starkey who is an earnest worker in the Wesleyan Sunday School, Latchford, gave his class a picnic to Chester on Thursday. About 50 friends including scholars left Wash Lane by bus at 8-30 arriving at the journey's end about noon. Dinner and tea were provided for the scholars and the day was spent by visiting the various places of interest in the city. 1.0.G.T. BONEHILL BRANCH LODGE, LATCHFORD. The usual weekly meeting of the above Order was held at the Temperance Hall, Latchford, on Monday evening., the chair being occupied by Bro. H. Richardson, C.T. After the usual business, there was an interesting programme, consisting of songs, solos, readings, etc. Afterwards, a farewell was taken of Bro. Howell who is leaving for South Wales.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF AN INFANT.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF AN INFANT.

Annie Mannion, aged two months, infant daugh- ter of Lawrence Mannion,a Ship Canal labourer, re- siding at 15, Morris's-court, off Church -st., died suddenly on Monday morning. Deceased was taken to bed by its mother on Sunday night at 9 45, and at about two o'clock on the following morning the mother awoke, laid it upon her arm.„ and went to sleep again. She awoke at 8' :39 and found her child lying dead upon her arm. A neighbour named Mrs. Bush was called in, and Dr. Jack was imme- diately sent for, who upon arriving pronounced life extimit. The child had been healthy since birth. The right side of deceased was discoloured.

div.head: STREET ACCIDENT.
div.p: STREET ACCIDENT.

On Wednesday afternoon a lurry belonging to Messrs. Buckley and Co., loaded with huge. Ameri- can baulks of timber, was being. driven through Scotland-road, at a somewhat rapid rate, when the end ot the lorry and one of the baulks caught the corner of Daley's lodging-house. The building was struck with such force that a longitudinal' fissure was made in the wall up to the level of the. bed- room windows, the crack indeed extending quite through it in some parts, and the window& being damaged. At present the corner does not strike one as being very safe, and pedestrians might do well to keep clear of it. THE RAGGED SUNDAY SCHOOL,

Anniversary services in connection with the above were held in the Public Hall, on Sunday. The sermons morning and evening were preached by the Rev. John Bennett, of Didsbury College. The musical portions of the service were rendered by the chillren, assisted by the choir of the Bank Quay Mission, under the leadership of Mr..P: ; Mr. J. Mills was at the organ. In the after- noon a service of song, entitled "The Wonderscpf Redeeming Grace," was given, Mr. Walter Brough being the reader. The congregation at each service was good. The collections amounted to XL% which, though less than last year, the Committee consider good evidence of the public appreciation of their work. THE TRADES' DEMONSTRATION,

div.head: WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB,
div.p: WARRINGTON CYCLING CLUB,

On Saturday the 25 miles road handicap of the above club was held. The course extended from the third milestone on the Knutsford-rd. to one mile past Lostock Gralam and back. The weather and roads were both excellent and a splendid race was witnessed. The following was the result :--lst W. F. Collier (2 minutes -start), 2nd J. Buxton (fl• minutes start), 3rd J. Waddington (14- minutes start), 4, J. Bellian (8f minutes start), and sth, W. 11. Bellian (scratch). W. F. Collier riding a Whippet pneumatic did the fastest time-1 hour, 23 minutes, 52 seconds, and W. H. Bellian on a R. and P. pneumatic did the 1 hour, 26, minutes, 244 seconds. Both these times beat the 25 miles record for last year ; but this season nothing short of 50' miles is considered a record for the road. All the live prize winners rode the dtstance under the Ll- hours showing that Warrington can stig turn out some smart men on the wheel, On Tuesday night the run was to Crontmt and about 15‘ members turned out, but the return journey was anything but pleasant owing to the heavy rain. Sr. MARY'S CATHOLIC CHURCH; BUTTRRMARKET,

div.head: STREET.
div.p: STREET.

On Sunday the great festival of Corpus Christi was celebrated at this church. At eleven o'clock: in the morning solemn high mass commenced, Father F. W. Sumner, 0.5.8., rector of St. Mary's,.officiating,, assisted by Father Duggan, as deacon,.and Father Turner sub-deacon. In the evening the greatest procession of the year took place, many little children taking part in it, dressed in white,.and carrying bouquets of flowers. The blessed sacra- ment was carried by Father Sumner,under a.canopy of white satin, the tour brass poles of the canopy being held by four non-commissioned officers from the barracks, eight other non-commissioned offibers ' walking at the end of the procession. The•choiT, under the leadership of Mr. Richard Etcles,, sang several selections of music during the procession round the church; and afterwards the benediction of the blessed sacrament was given by Father Sumner, assisted by Father Turner, as deacon, and Father Duggan as sub-deacon. The children, with their tine banners, were grouped around the high altar and side chapels during the benediction service, and the scene was very imposing. The altars were adorned with the choicest flowers.. MR. T. MORRIS ON CHURCH ATTRNDANCI4-

On Sunday, Mr. and Mrs. Thomas, Morris pre- sented the prizes to the girls and boys attending All Saints' Mission Sunday School, lityle-st., off Beaysey-road. Mr. Morrie addressed, the scholars upon the importance of attending a place of wor- ship after they had left the Sabbath school. He re- marked that he and: Mrs. Morris had attended the services at St. Paul'S Church for the past years, and he did not think the attendance had increased at all during that period. During that time from 2,000 to 3,000 boys. and girls had passed through their schools and had become men and women, and it was a matter of wrprise to him that, although so many children had attended the Sunday schools, when they left, they should never afterwards go to a place of worship. Surely the Sunday school should be the natural feeder ot the places of wor- ship, and although worshippers died, those who had been Sunday school scholars should more than replace them. Instead of" empty pews being the rule in their churches they should be the exception. There were some people who contended that to be religious and atten&Sunday services was expensive. That, however, was not the case. It was far more expensive to linger about for the public-house doors to be opened, or to drive about the country. The Sabbath should, he contended, be kept in a becom- • ing manner, as "A Sabbath well spent brings a week of content." Mr. Morris complimented the children upon the improvement which had taken place in their conduct. A good deal was owing to the care which had been exercised by Mr. Sudlow, who ap- peared to be an excellent superintendent. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr. and Mrs. Morris for their services, on the motion of the Vicar of St. Paul's, the Rev, H. V. Pigot. and the proceedings terminated.

GREAT STORM IN THE MMLANDS. A storm of exceptional severity passed over Derby- shire, on Thursday, and the low-lying parts are Blooded. A Brampton boy was drowsed. THE STEAMER ALBERT BIJRNT. Yesterday the Penzance steamer Albert was towed to Portland Roads, on fire, The fire was extinguished', but the vessel is almost a total wreck.

THE WELSH TRAGEDY'. Yesterday, Duncan was committed to trial for the attempted murder of his wife in North Ws.lns-. Mrs. Duncan remains in a critical condition. THE BACCAAIT SCANDAL. Yesterday the hearing of the baccarat action was resumed before Chief Justice Coleridge. The Prince of Wales was again present. Mrs. Lycett Green's cross- examination having concluded, Mrs. Arthur Wilson, hostess at Tranby Croft, was sworn. She said her son mentioned cheating on thc . first evening she watched Sir William. She noticed then that he was cheating, and wondered that others did not notice it. Lord Coventry, the next witness, said when he told plaintiff people were talking about his conduct, he replied, " Good God,what do you mean? What do they say ? " Lord Coventry was under cross-examination when the Court adjourned for luncheon.

THE LIVERPOOL MURDER. John Conway was on Thursday charged before the Liverpool stipendiary with the murder of the boy Nicholas Martin. Mr. Tetlow, prisoner's solicitor, wrote announ- cing his withdrawl from the case. The evidence was the same as that given at the inquest. The prisoner cross- examined several of the witnesses very closely as to the exact times they had seen him. After 'questioning the labourer Thomas Hankey, who saw him talking to the boy he called him a white-livered scoundrel, and prayed that the curse of God might rest on him. Afterwards cross- examining the boy James Phillipin, who witnessed the placing of the bag in the hansom, prisoner used the ex- pression " he " in reference to the person seen by the witness. Mr. Stewart, stipendiary, asked the prisoner whom he meant by " ; whereupon Conway said, "I sin not going to say I am the man; I would 'sooner a thunderbolt came down and struck me." The case was adjourned until next day. Yesterday, Conway was committed for triat for the murder of the boy Martin. CONDITION OF THE CANADIAN PREMIER. OTTAWA, THURSDAY MIDNIGHT.—EO-Dight the Premier's general condition is much as it was yesterday at the same liGur, excepting that the heart's action is weaker and still more irregular. The respiration is 30 and pulse 100.

YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The Lord Chancellor took his seat on the woolsack at a quarter past four. The Behring Sea Seal Fishery 13111 was read a first time. Lord LIERSCHILL drew attention to the punish- ment of habitual drunkards and moved for an inquiry into the subject which was agreed to. The House adjourned at 5.20 p.m. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The Speaker took the chair at four minutes past three o'clock. THE SHIP CANAL BILL.—On the motion of Mr. • RITCHIB the Select Committee on the Manchester Ship Canal Bill was neminated as follows :—Mr. Barren, Mr. Leng, Mr. Llinckes, and Sir Richard Temple, with three members to be added by the Committee of Selection. IRISH LAND BILL.—Mr. W. H. SMITH having stated that there was no foundation for the rumours abroad as to the autumn session the House went into Committee on the Land Purchase Bill and proceeded to consideration of a now clause, moved by Mr. LEA, designed to retain in their offices existing land commission as appointed under former land acts.

Shoulders move more freely than of late. Cheese remains steady, with a moderate inquiry, new makes still being most sought after. Butter is nominal. TRH FATAL FALL.

An inquest was held at the St. Helens•Town Hall, on Friday, before Mr. Samuel Brighouse, Eoron or of South- West Lancashire, on the body of William Kay, 54. years of age, a stone non, of Wavertree, who was killed by falling from a platform at the chemical' works of Messrs. MTryde,St. Helens. on Wednesday. The deceased was in the employ of Mr. Peter Rigby, a St. Helens contractor, and was repairing a condenser. He stood on a platform 14ft. from the ground,and suddenly fell back- wards. He alighted on his head, his skull tieing frac- tured, and death was instantaneous. Mr. J. P. Mearns appeared on behalf of Mr. Rigby, and it was stated that the deceased had been in Mr. Rigby's employ for 18 or 19 years, and was an experienced man at the work, A verdict of "Accidental death was returned,

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. TO TIIE ELECTORS OF WHITECROSS WARD. LADIES AND GENT'LEMEN,—A vacancy has been caused in Your Ward through the elevation of Councillor Greenall to the Aldermanic Bench, and, as I have been requested by a large number of ratepayers to become a candidate for the vacant Pest, I beg to offer myself for your suffrages. I think I may Claim to be well-known to most of you as a resident in the Ward. I am glad to see that the Baths are to be enlarged and , Unproved. I am of opinion that steps should be taken to effect a reduction in the price of Gas ; and I am in favour of a Stipendiary Magistrate, if an appointment can be made Without being a burden on the rates. I am strongly of opinion that there should be a Public Inquiry as to the Intercepting Depots and Longford Works. TeY judgment, the, ratepayers are at all times entitled to Ilaye their grievances inquired into, and to know how their bleney is being spent. At the same time, I am desirous 13( assisting the Sanitary Committee in dealing with insanitary 4Wellings, and doing what they can to make the homes of Working-men healthier and more comfortable. Trusting to obtain your support on the day of election, I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, GEO. PLUMPTON. 225, Lovely-lane, Warrington, June sth, 1891.

MUNICIPAL ELECTION. WHITECROSS WARD. TO TUE BURG ESSES OF THE WARD. LADIEs ANDGENTLEXEN,—At the invitation a a large and influential body of ratepayers, I have much pleasure in again offering myself for election as your representative, on Mon- day, June 15th. I have, as many of you know, for over ten years taken an active part and interest in all matters calcu- lated to benefit the ratepayers generally, and to improve our town. Being a resident in your Ward, as well as a native of War- tington, my interests and yours are the same ; you may therefore depend upon my giving my best attention to all Matters promoted to improve the streets, and working-men's dwellings in the Ward. lam strongly in favour of all Cor- Poration contracts being given to Warrington men, and that RIO tender be accepted where sweating is carried on. I am most favourably dispoaed towards large and commo- -4°hs baths being erected at once, and opened free on certain uaYs to all school children under control of their teachers ; and also that the prices charged, especially for the swimming baths, shall be as low as possible, so as to encourage the art Of swimming amongst all, which is now impossible, owing to the Prohibitive charge. I pledge myself, if jetuzned, to *hake it my aim, at all times, to bring forward 4nd support measures calculated to secure the greatest com- fort and c9uvenience of the Burgesses. I am, yours faithfully, ALFRED WOODS. 98. Bewsey-road, Warrington, June 50, 1891.

The Directors have the pleasure to report that after making ample provision for all bad and doubtful debts, and providing for the rebate of discount on current bills, the profits for the year 1890, including £54,706 14s. 6d. brought forward, amount to £565,048 14s. From this sum the Directors have transferred £25,000 to credit of Bank Premises Account, and £lO,OOO to the Bank's Benevolent Fund. The Directors recommend that a bonus of 6 per cent, be paid, free of Income TaY, to the Proprietors in July next (making, with the dividends and bonus already paid, 20 per cent, for the year). and that the balance of £74,892 9s. be carried to the profits of 1891. The Share Capital issued last year has been fully sub- scribed, and the amount received for premiums on the sale of the 2,500 unappropriated Shares credited to the Bank's Premises Account, in accordance with the last Annual report. During the year Branches have been opened at Warring- ton and in Finchley Road, llampstead, both of which will, it is expected, prove advantageous to the Bank and useful to its customers. In conjunction with the Bank of England and the leading Banking and Financial Institutions throughout the King- dom, this Bank joined, to the extent of £750,000, in a guar- antee in connection with the liquidation by the Bank of England of the estate of Messrs. Baring Brothers and Co., the Directors believing it to be to the general interests of the country that the threatened crisis and consequent injury to credit should be prevented. The Directors retiring by rotation are :—Duxclx MAC- DONALD, ESQ., GEORGE FORBES MALCOLMSON, Esq., MAURICE OTHO FITZGERALD, ESQ., all of whom, being eligible, offer themselves for re-election. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.—CONTRACT FOR SUP- PLY OF COALS AND SLACK. The School Manage- ment Committee are prepared to receive TENDERS for the supply of coals and slack for use in the Board Schools, from July Ist, 1881, to the Ist July, 1892. Tenders, endorsed " Tender for Fuel," stating quality and the several prices per ton (to be delivered free at the Schools), must be sent in to the undersigned on or before noon, June 23rd, 1891. The Committee do not bind themselves to recommend the accept- ance of the lowest or any tender. By order. G. H DANDY, Clerk to the Board. Town Hall, Widnes, 3rd June, 1891.

DRESCOT UNION.—CONTRACTS FOR PROVISIONS, &c.• Persons desirous of contracting with the Guardians of this Union, for the next Six Months, for supplying at the Workhouse the several articles hereinafter named, viz., Flour, Oatmeal, Salt Butter, Margarine, Cheese, Eggs, Groceries, Coal, Linen and Woollen Drapery. Smallwares, Tinware, Hardware, Ironmongery, Earthenware, Boots and Shoes, Leather. Hay and Straw. Brushes, Coffins, and other articles, are requested to deliver Sealed Tenders, upon Forms to be obtained at my office at the Boardroom of the said Union. in Whiston, on or before Thursday. the 18th June, before 10 a.m. Such Tenders will be opened at the meeting of the Guardians on the last-named day. The Guardians will also take Tenders for New Milk and Fresh Butter for Twelve Months. Samples of unperishable articles required may be seen at the Workhouse, Security will be required for the performance of the contracts. The Guardians do not bind themselves to accept the lowest or any tender. By order of the Board, A. F. MANN, Union Clerk. Union Offices, Whiston, Prescot, 4th June, 1891.

PITCH AND Toss.—William Sandbach, a boatman, was ordered to pay the costs, 4s. 6d., for playing pitch and toss. AN. UNMANAGABLB Bor.—William Houghton, aged 12, was charged with sleeping in the works of Mesirs. Wigg Bros.and Steele. The father said he could not manage the lad who was sent to the Workhouse for a week. SCIIOOL BOARD PROSECIITIONS.—A number of parents were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case. -- WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TRIIRSDAY.—Before Mr. T. S. Timmis, and Mr. J. Birchall. MISCEILLANBOVS.—An old offender named Rose Kelly, was fined 10s. and costs for trespassing on the London and North-Western Railway at Widnes. The defendant had passed beneath the couplings of a train at Anne-st. Crossing.—For playing pitch and toss at Ditton, four young Irishmen were each fined 6d. and costs.—Michael Percival, Margaret Forbes, Sarah Naughton, and Catherine Sweeney, were each bound over to be of good behaviour for three months for creating a breach of the peace.—Samuel Johnson was charged with having been asleep on his cart on the 26th May, but as there was a doubt in the case, he was dismissed. &moor. BOARD PROSECIITIONS.—A number of parents were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school and the usual fine of 6d. and costs was imposed in each case. Tanpr.—Eliza Drury, and Mary Allen, girls, were charged with stealing three quarters of a hundred weight of coal from the canal bank at Whines, the property of the London and North-Western Railway Company, on the 29th May.—P.C. Tweddle caught the prisoners in the act of stealing the coal and apprehended them. As the girls had been in prison since apprehended the Bench thought they would be sufficiently punished by the sen- tence of one day's imprisonment.
